1. General [Section]
1.1.(1) Summary of the Treatise (Śāstrasaṃgraha) 1.1.5.

Having created living beings, Prajāpati first proclaimed to them, in one hundred thousand chapters, the means for accomplishing the three aims of life (*trivarga*) as the basis for their stability. 1.1.6.
Manu Svāyambhuva composed a separate work based on a portion of that [original treatise], concerning the subject of *dharma*.
1.1.8. Nandin, a follower of Mahādeva, separately proclaimed a *Kāmasūtra* consisting of one thousand chapters.
(p. 4) 1.1.9. Śvetaketu, the son of Uddālaka, then abridged that very work into five hundred chapters.

(p. 4) 1.1.10. Furthermore, he [Vātsyāyana] again condensed that same work into one hundred and fifty chapters, divided into the following sections: *Sādhāraṇa*, *Sāṃprayogika*, *Kanyāsaṃprayuktaka*, *Bhāryādhikārika*, *Pāradārika*, and *Vaiśika*.
Bābhravya Pāñcāla, a follower of the Upaniṣads, condensed [the science] into seven sections.
Of that work, Dattaka composed a separate sixth section on courtesans (*vaiśika*) at the request of the courtesans of Pāṭaliputra.
Following that context, Cārāyaṇa separately expounded a section on common women (*sādhāraṇa*).
Suvarṇanābha [deals with] matters concerning sexual union; Ghoṭakamukha, matters concerning courtesans;
Gonardīya, matters concerning wives.
Goṇikāputra [composed] the section on adultery;
Kucumāra, the section on secret doctrines (*aupaniṣadika*).
Thus, that treatise, composed in fragments by many teachers, became nearly lost.

1.1.14. Among those [works], because the treatises composed by Dattaka and others consist of only single parts of the science, and because the work of Bābhravya, though extensive, is difficult to study, this *Kāmasūtra* has been composed, condensing the entire subject matter into a brief text. 1.2.(2) The Pursuit of the Three Aims of Life (Trivarga). 1.2.1. A man’s lifespan is indeed one hundred years; having divided this time, he should pursue the three aims of life—which are interconnected and do not conflict with one another—without allowing them to harm each other. (p. 10) 1.2.2. In childhood, he should attend to matters such as the acquisition of knowledge. (p. 10)
1.2.3. And one may pursue sensual pleasure in youth; 1.2.4. Dharma and liberation in old age;
1.2.5. Or, because life is impermanent, one may practice whichever [of these] occurs first.
1.2.6. Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) indeed [is required] until the acquisition of knowledge.
1.2.7. Sacrifices and the like, which do not pertain to worldly life and whose purpose is unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), are set in motion by the scripture for those who would otherwise not engage in them;
whereas [actions] pertaining to worldly life... [are set in motion] because they are worldly.

Because it pertains to worldly matters and concerns visible purposes, the restraint from meat-eating and other such activities—once they have been undertaken—is *dharma* solely by virtue of the scripture.
(1.2.8) One should understand that [dharma] through the revealed word (*śruti*) and from an assembly of those who know *dharma*.
(1.2.9) *Artha* is the acquisition of knowledge, land, gold, cattle, grain, utensils, equipment, friends, and so forth, as well as the increase of what has been acquired. (1.2.10)
1.2.10. [This is to be known] from the conduct of superintendents, from those who know the conventions of trade, and from merchants.

(p.13) 1.2.11. Desire (*kāma*) is the functioning of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose—presided over by the mind (*manas*) conjoined with the self (*ātman*)—toward their respective objects in accordance with one's own inclination. (p.13) 1.2.12. However, because it is accompanied by the pleasure of self-conceit (*abhimānika-sukha*), the fruitful cognition of an object arising from the specific quality of touch is primarily desire. (p.14)
1.2.13. One should learn this from the *Kāmasūtra* and from the assemblies of city-dwellers.
1.2.14. Among these sources, each preceding one is more authoritative than the following.
1.2.15. And it is for the sake of the king’s interest.
Since the course of worldly life is rooted in that [the three aims], and since the courtesan is also included therein, there is the attainment of the *trivarga* (the three aims of life). 1.2.16.
Because *dharma* is not of this world (*alaukika*), it is appropriate that there be a scripture (*śāstra*) to explain it.
Since the accomplishment of an object depends on the prior application of means, the understanding of those means is derived from the treatise (śāstra).
(1.2.16) However, the teachers maintain that because desire operates spontaneously even among animals and because it is constant, there is no need for a treatise [in this regard]. (1.2.17)
1.2.18. Because sexual union depends upon mutual cooperation, it requires a specific method (*upāya*).
1.2.19. Vātsyāyana maintains that the knowledge of how to apply this method is derived from the *Kāmasūtra*.
1.2.20. Furthermore, because the female species is not restricted to a single womb among the three types of wombs (*tri-yag-yoni*), [the method is necessary].

Because activity during the fertile period is for the sake of a specific purpose, and because such activities are not preceded by conscious deliberation, the resulting cognition is not a valid means of knowledge.
(p.17) 1.2.21: "One should not practice dharma, because its fruit is yet to come."
And because it involves uncertainty: (p.18) 1.2.22. For what person, unless he were a fool, would allow that which is already in his hand to pass into the hands of another?
(p.18) 1.2.23. A pigeon today is better than a peacock tomorrow. (p.19)
1.2.24. "A certain kārṣāpaṇa is better than a doubtful niṣka"—thus say the Lokāyatikas.
[This is because] the scripture is beyond suspicion, and because the results of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) and incantations (*anuvyāhāra*) are occasionally observed.

Vātsyāyana maintains that one should practice dharma because we observe the movement of the circle of constellations, the moon, the sun, the stars, and the planets as if it were preceded by intelligence for the sake of the world; because the course of worldly life is characterized by the maintenance of the conduct of the social classes and stages of life; and because we see the abandonment of seed in hand for the sake of the future harvest.
1.2.26. One should not pursue material objects, for even when these are pursued with great effort, they may never come to pass.
Even those things that occur by chance, though not being intentionally performed,
all arise through the action of Time (kāla).
For it is Time alone that establishes men in prosperity or adversity, victory or defeat, and pleasure or pain.
1.2.29. By time Bali was made Indra; by time he was deposed.
"Time alone shall act upon him again"—thus say those who hold time to be the cause (kālakāraṇika).
(1.2.30) Because all activities are preceded by human effort (puruṣakāra), the means (upāya) is the decisive factor (pratyaya).
(1.2.31) For even an event that is destined to happen necessarily occurs only through the employment of a means.
"There is no welfare for one who is inactive," says Vātsyāyana (1.2.32).
One should not pursue sensual desires,
because they are antagonistic to dharma and artha, which are the primary goals, as well as to other virtuous qualities.
These [vices] produce for a man association with harmful people, improper exertion, impurity, and lack of future security (1.2.33).
Likewise, they produce negligence, levity, lack of trustworthiness, and unacceptability (1.2.34).
Moreover, it is heard that many who were under the sway of desire perished along with their entire retinues.
1.2.35. Just as the Bhoja king named Dāṇḍakya, through lust, perished along with his kinsmen and his kingdom after lusting after a Brahmin maiden;

(p. 24) 1.2.36. And the King of the Gods [Indra] for Ahalyā, the exceedingly powerful Kīcaka for Draupadī, Rāvaṇa for Sītā, and many others besides—those who contemplate the nature of things observe that these and many more were destroyed when they fell under the sway of desire.
(p. 24) 1.2.37. For desires share the same nature as food, insofar as they are the cause for the maintenance of the body.
And [the means] are the fruits of the Dharma and its purpose (p. 25, 1.2.38).
But one must understand that [the means] are like [the avoidance of] faults:
for it is not because there are no beggars that cooking pots are not placed on the fire.
Vātsyāyana maintains that it is not the case that because deer do not exist, barley is not consumed.
And there are verses on this point: A man who thus pursues wealth, pleasure, and virtue enjoys ultimate happiness, free from all thorns, both in this world and the next.

A man should study the Kāmasūtra and its auxiliary sciences without neglecting the time allotted to the Vedas, material wealth, and the auxiliary sciences of Dharma. (p. 27)
1.3.2. Before puberty, a woman [is under her father's authority], and after marriage, she is under the will of her husband.
1.3.3. Since women lack the capacity to grasp the treatises, the teachers maintain that instruction for women is useless in this treatise. (p. 27)
1.3.4. Vātsyāyana, however, maintains that the mention of "practice" (prayoga) refers to these [arts], because practice is preceded by the study of the treatise (śāstra). 1.3.5.
This [principle] applies not only here.
For in every part of the world, there are only a few who are experts in the treatises (*śāstra*), yet linguistic usage (*prayoga*) pertains to all people.
And for such usage, even a treatise that is remote in time is indeed the authority (*hetu*). (1.3.6) (p. 28)

1.3.7. Even those who are not grammarians, such as ritualists, employ the *ūha* (adaptation) in sacrifices, thinking, "Grammar exists. 1.3.8. Thinking, "Astronomy exists," they perform rituals on auspicious days.
1.3.9. Likewise, horse-riders and elephant-riders train horses and elephants even without having mastered the technical treatises [on their subjects].
1.3.10. Just as even those living in distant provinces do not overstep the boundaries [of the kingdom] because "there is a king," so it is with this [the science of love].
1.3.11. Indeed, there are courtesans, princesses, and daughters of high officials whose intellects have been refined by the study of the treatises.
1.3.12. Therefore, in private, a woman should acquire the entire treatise or at least a portion of it from a trustworthy person through practical application.

1.3.13. A maiden, alone and in secret, should practice the sixty-four arts that require repeated application. 1.3.14. (4) The Conduct of the Urban Dwellers (nāgaraka-vṛtta). 1.4.1 / Having acquired learning and entered the householder stage by means of wealth obtained through gifts, conquest, purchase, or inheritance, or by both ancestral and self-acquired means, one should conduct oneself according to the conduct of an urban dweller. 1.4.2. One should establish a residence in a city, a port, a market town, or a large settlement frequented by virtuous people, or else in accordance with the requirements of one's travels.

Social gatherings,

Having experienced the daily excursion there, they should pass the time with cockfights, gambling, spectacles, and agreeable diversions; then, in the afternoon, having taken the marks of their enjoyment of those gardens, they should return in the same manner. 1.4.31. But the *pīṭhamarda* is one who lacks wealth, possessing only his body and such meager belongings as a *mallikā* garland, soap-powder, and astringent dyes;

having come from a respectable region and being skilled in the arts, he maintains himself through their instruction in social circles and in conduct appropriate for the *veśa*. 1.4.32. The *viṭa*, however, is one whose wealth has been consumed, yet who is virtuous, accompanied by a wife, highly esteemed in the *veśa* and in social circles, and subsists upon that [wealth].

or he may be a Vaihāsika (jester).
1.4.34. These serve as counselors to courtesans and city-dwellers, being appointed to manage peace and war.
1.4.35. By these [rules], female mendicants who are skilled in the arts, shaven-headed women, low-caste women, and elderly courtesans are explained.

1.4.36. A village-dweller, having encouraged his kinsmen who are discerning and curious, should describe the conduct of the city-folk, generating faith in them, and imitate that very same conduct himself.
He should also initiate social gatherings (*goṣṭhī*).
One should please people through association, assist them in their undertakings,

In connection with giving that [gift], there should be a kiss from her that is gentle, clear, and not hurried.
3.2.13. There, he should converse with a woman who has attained proficiency.
3.2.14. For the purpose of hearing her speak, he should ask about some trivial matter of few syllables, as if he were ignorant of it.
3.2.15. Without causing her distress when she shows no understanding, he should ask repeatedly, employing soothing words.
3.2.16. Even in such a case, one should press her for an answer while she remains silent.
3.2.17. For all young women endure the speech employed by a man;
however, they do not utter even words that are light or mixed with triviality.
Thus says Ghoṭakamukha.
(p.201) 3.2.18. But when being pressed for an answer, one should provide replies by nodding the head;
however, in a quarrel, one should not nod the head. (p.202)

3.2.19. When asked, "Do you desire me or not? Are you pleased with me or not? she should remain silent for a long time; then, when pressed, she should nod her head in compliance. But if she is being probed further, she should dispute the matter. 3.2.20. If she is well-acquainted [with the suitor], she should interpose a trusted female friend who is equally confident on both sides and engage in conversation through her.
She should laugh with her face turned downward;
and she should revile and dispute with that woman who speaks excessively.
She, however, should say—even if it were not said—that "this was spoken by her for the sake of jest."
In that situation, having set aside her [anger], she should remain silent when entreated for a reply;
but if she is pressed further, she should speak words with indistinct syllables and incomplete meaning, saying, "I do not say such a thing."
And sometimes, smiling, she might glance at the hero with sidelong looks;
such is the application of conversation. (p.
203) 3.2.21. And when familiarity has thus arisen, without speaking directly, she should place near him the betel-leaf, ointment, and garland that he has requested.
Or he should tie it to her upper garment.
3.2.22. When she is thus engaged, he should touch the two bud-like breasts with a light stroke (ācchuritaka).
3.2.23. Even if she resists, saying, "You too must embrace me, then I shall not act in this way," he should cause her to embrace him by remaining firm.
He should extend his own hand down to the region of her navel and withdraw it;
then, having gradually raised her onto his lap, he should proceed with increasing intensity.
And if she does not yield, he should frighten her.
"3.2.24. 'Indeed, I shall place tooth-marks upon your lower lip and nail-marks upon the surface of your breasts;
and having done this myself, I shall tell your circle of friends that it was done by you.
What will you say to them about this?'—with such childish threats and means of convincing the naive, she should gradually deceive her."
3.2.25. On the second and third nights, when she has become somewhat more confident, he should take hold of her with his hand.
3.2.26. He should begin with kissing that involves all parts of the body.
3.2.27. Having placed his hands upon her thighs, once the act of massaging is mastered, he should gradually massage even the root of the thighs.
If she should agitate him by asking, "What is the fault in ceasing the massage?",
he should steady her; then,
once she has been won over, there is the touching of the secret parts.
3.2.28. Unfastening the girdle, loosening the knot of the lower garment, changing the clothing, and massaging the root of the thighs—
these are his other pretexts.
One should make her devoted by providing her with appropriate means,
but one must not break one's vow at an improper time. And one should instruct her.
One should demonstrate one's own affection,
recount former desires,
and pledge one's future conduct in accordance with those [desires].
She should dispel her fear of rival wives;
and when she has gradually become free from her maidenhood, he should approach her without causing her distress—
thus is the winning of the girl's confidence.
And there are verses on this point:
"In this way, one who follows the mind should win over a young woman through skillful means;
thus she becomes both devoted to him and full of confidence."

3.2.31ab. Neither by excessive compliance nor by extreme opposition does one attain success with maidens; therefore, one should achieve it through the middle way. 3.2.31cd. [This way] generates pleasure for oneself and increases the self-esteem of women. 3.2.32ab. [It is] that which produces joy for oneself and increases the pride of women.
3.2.32cd. He who knows how to inspire confidence in a maiden shall become dear to her. 3.2.33ab. But he who neglects a maiden, thinking, "She is possessed of excessive modesty," [will not win her].

3.2.33cd. He, being ignorant of her intentions, is treated with contempt like an animal. 3.2.34ab. Or, if she is approached by force by one who has not discerned her heart, 3.2.34cd. She immediately experiences fear, terror, agitation, and hatred.
3.2.35ab. Failing to attain union with him in love, she may be corrupted by that agitation; 3.2.35cd. she may become a hater of men, or, being repulsed, she may go to another.
3.3. Initiatory approaches toward a young girl and the indication of her gestures and expressions.
3.3.1. But one who is devoid of wealth, even if endowed with virtues,
or one who possesses neutral qualities or a low reputation,
or a wealthy neighbor;
Dependent upon his mother, father, and brothers, or following the conduct of a child, he may not choose a maiden for himself because she is unavailable;
therefore, from her childhood onwards, he himself should cultivate an affection for her. 3.3.2.

3.3.3. Acting thus, following the family of his maternal uncle in the Deccan while still a boy, separated from both mother and father, and treated as if he were insignificant, he should win over the daughter of his maternal uncle—unobtainable due to her great wealth—or another girl previously given to someone else.
3.3.4. He may even desire another woman who is an outsider.
3.3.5. "When this is the case, enchantment (*saṃvanana*) is praiseworthy for the attainment of one's purpose with a young girl," says Ghoṭakamukha.

(p.208) 3.3.6. Together with her, he should engage in gathering flowers, weaving garlands, playing in the house, arranging games for the daughter, and preparing food and drink, in accordance with their familiarity and age.

3.3.7. She should play with him at games such as *ākarṣa* (pulling), *paṭṭikā* (board-games), *muṣṭi-dyūta* (fist-fighting), *kṣullaka* (small dice), and other such games; at the game of grasping the middle finger (*madhyamāṅguligrahaṇa*); and at regional games such as *ṣaṭ-pāṣāṇaka* (the six-stone game). Out of a sense of familiarity with these, she should play together with him using female slaves and maidservants who are well-acquainted with them. 3.3.8. With her friends, she should engage in other regional games such as *kṣveḍitaka* (shouting challenges), *sunimīlitaka* (blindman's buff), *ārabdhikā* (starting a race), *lavaṇavīthikā* (the salt-path game), *anilatāḍitaka* (the wind-blown game), *godhūmapuñjikā* (the wheat-heap game), and *aṅgulitāḍitaka* (the finger-tapping game).

3.3.9. And with whichever woman of this [harem] he might feel confidence, he should cultivate an uninterrupted intimacy with her and observe her habits. 3.3.10. He should also treat her nurse-maid more than usual with kindness and for her benefit.
For she, being affectionate and having recognized his intentions, might be able to unite him with her even without being asked;
yet, even if not requested, she would not refuse the role of preceptor.
For even one who has not discerned his intentions may reveal his virtues out of affection.
He should act in such a way that the woman to be employed becomes enamored. Wherever there is an object of curiosity for her, he should enter into that and accomplish it for her.
He should procure for her, without effort, those playthings which are unprecedented and rare among other women.
3.3.14. There, she should display various balls, variegated with many patterns, changing from one to another at short intervals.
Likewise, she should show dolls made of thread, wood, cow-hair, and ivory, as well as those made of beeswax, flour, and clay.
3.3.15. She should also display a large iron pan for the purpose of cooking rice.

3.3.16. And [theft] of wood and phalli; of women and men joined in union; of goats and sheep; of temples and houses constructed of clay, split bamboo, or wood; of cages for parrots, cuckoos, love-birds, mainas, quails, cocks, and partridges, fashioned with various forms; and of water-vessels, mechanical toys, lutes, and flutes.

He should provide secret gifts of lac, red arsenic, yellow orpiment, vermilion, black pigments, and the like, as well as sandalwood, saffron, betel nuts, and leaves when appropriate for the season, within the limits of his capacity; and he should give openly those items that are publicly known.
He should strive in such a way that the recipient considers him to be fulfilling all of his desires.
3.3.17. And while looking at her, he should request her in secret; likewise, he should engage in conversation with her in secret.
3.3.18. As for the reason for giving gifts in secret, he should proclaim his fear of his elders.
And [he should ensure] that the donor becomes desirable to others.
3.3.19. He should delight her, whose affection is increasing, with narratives that are meaningful and captivating to the mind. 3.3.20.
When she is overcome by wonder, he should astonish her with applications of magical illusions (*indrajāla*).
To her who is curious about the arts, he should please her through skill in those arts; to her who loves song, with songs that captivate the ear;

during the festival of the moon in the month of Āśvayuja, during the Kaumudī festival, on processions, at eclipses, or during domestic rites—with various flower-garlands, ear-ornaments fashioned from leaf-patterns, and gifts of beeswax, garments, rings, and jewelry.
If he does not consider them to be harmful,
then, because she is well-acquainted with the particularities of other men, he should have her nurse teach her the sixty-four arts (cātuḥṣaṣṭika-yoga) regarding the conduct of men.
And by instructing her in their mastery, he should demonstrate his own skill in the art of love toward the woman to be won over.

3.3.23. He himself should be elegantly dressed and possess an unimpaired appearance; furthermore, he should indicate her state of mind through gestures and outward expressions. 3.3.24. For young women first desire a man with whom they have become acquainted and who is seen frequently.
"Even though they desire him, they do not make advances"—this is a general observation.
Thus end the approaches toward a young girl. (p.
211) 3.3.25. We shall now describe those gestures and outward signs. (p. 214)
3.3.26. However, she does not look him directly in the face; when looked at, she shows bashfulness;
and she reveals her own attractive limb under some pretext.
She observes the leader when he is negligent, concealed, or has transgressed;
and when asked something, she speaks very softly with her face cast downward, smiling faintly and using indistinct syllables whose meaning is not fully expressed;
furthermore, she delights in staying near him for a long time.
Thinking, "Let her see me while standing at a distance," she addresses her attendants with a change of facial expression and does not leave that spot;
whatever she sees, she laughs. 3.3.28.
There, she engages in conversation for the sake of establishing a connection;
she embraces and kisses the young boy who has come into her lap,
and she applies a sectarian mark upon the servant girl.
She restrains her attendants and displays various graceful gestures;
she places her trust in his friends and highly values their speech, acting upon it.
He engages in pleasure, conversation, and gambling with his attendants;
he appoints them to their respective tasks as if he were their master;
and when they are engaged in conversation about their leader or speak of someone else, he listens attentively to that talk.
3.3.30. Urged by her foster-sister, she enters the hero's residence;
desiring to place her between them, she wishes to engage in gambling, play, and conversation with him, yet remains unadorned when within his sight.
She avoids [wearing] earrings, a ring, or a garland; when requested by him, she calmly removes them from her body and places them in the hand of her female friend.
And she always wears what has been given by him.
She becomes despondent during conversations concerning other suitors and does not associate with those who belong to their faction.
And on this matter, you have two verses:
Having observed these outward forms and gestures associated with her internal state,
one should contemplate various means for the sake of union with the maiden.

3.3.32ab. A girl who plays with children's toys when she is young, and remains [interested] in the arts when she has reached youth; 3.3.32cd. And one who is affectionate—such a woman should be won over by winning over those people in whom she trusts. (p.216) 3.4. Approaches by a single man.
3.4.1. When a maiden has revealed her gestures and outward expressions, one should approach her by means of a stratagem.
3.4.2. While disputing during a game of dice or other playthings, he should take hold of her hand with a significant gesture.
3.4.3. And one should perform the methods of embracing, such as the "touching" (spṛṣṭaka) and so forth, as previously described.
(p. 216) 3.4.4. And during the practice of leaf-cutting (patracchedya), one should show her a couple that indicates one's own intention.
(p. 217) 3.4.5. In this manner, one should show other things sparingly. (p. 217)

3.4.6. During water-sports, having submerged herself in the water at a distance from him, she should approach him, touch him, and then surface right there. 3.4.7. And through [the exchange of] fresh leaves and such items, she should communicate her special state of feeling. 3.4.9. And by means of a pretext, she should mention a dream characterized by her feelings.
3.4.10. During a theatrical performance or in a gathering of kinsmen, she should sit close by him; there, under some pretext, she should touch him.
(p. 217) 3.4.11. And for the sake of support, she should press her foot against his foot. (p. 217)
3.4.12. Then, he should gradually touch each finger one by one.
3.4.13. And with the big toe, he should rub the tips of the nails. 3.4.14. When successful in that, he should desire to advance further from step to step.
3.4.15. And for the sake of practicing forbearance, one should practice that very same thing.
3.4.16. During the washing of the feet, there is the pressing of the toes with the space between the toes.
3.4.17. During the offering or the receiving of an object, there is a physical transformation occurring therein.
3.4.19. Sitting in pairs in a secluded place and in the dark, one should practice patience, as well as when sharing the same location and bed. (p.
218) 3.4.20. In that regard, for one who does not cause agitation, there is the disclosure of one's inner state according to the facts. (p. 219)

3.4.21. Having said, "There is something to be told in private," she should observe his speech and his disposition there. As we shall explain regarding the wife of another (in sūtra 3.4.26). 3.4.22. But once her feelings are known, he, under the pretext of illness, should bring her to his own residence for the purpose of receiving news.

3.4.23. When she has arrived, he should direct her to massage his head; taking hold of her hand, he should place it expressively upon her eyes and forehead. (p. 219) 3.4.24. And under the pretext of medicine, he should prescribe a treatment for her. (p. 219)

3.4.25. "This must be performed by you; for this cannot be accomplished by anyone other than a maiden. Having said this, he should dismiss her as she departs, with the condition that she must return. (p. 220) 3.4.26. And the application of this practice is for three nights and at the three junctions of the day. (p. 220)
3.4.27. And for one who has come for the purpose of frequent meetings, he should increase the social circle.
(p.220) 3.4.28. Even with other women, he should apply himself more and more for the sake of gaining her confidence, but he must not speak disparagingly of her. (p.220)

3.4.29. "Even when a man has traveled far away, he does not succeed with maidens through despondency," says Ghoṭakamukha. (p. 220) 3.4.30. But when he considers her to be highly accomplished, only then should he begin his advances. (p. 220) 3.4.31. At twilight, at night, and in the darkness, women have little apprehension regarding sexual union. (p. 220)
They are resolute and full of passion, and they do not reject a man; therefore, it is the common saying that she should be employed at that time. (p. 221)

3.4.32. However, if a single man’s advances are impossible, she should, by means of a nurse’s daughter or a female friend who has been won over and is integrated into her circle, have that matter conveyed to him without speaking of it directly; then, together with her, she should approach him as prescribed.
(p. 221) 3.4.33. Or, she should from the very beginning establish one of her own female attendants in the position of a friend to this woman. (p. 221)

3.4.34. At a sacrifice, a wedding, a journey, a festival, or during a time of misfortune; when people are occupied with spectacles or elsewhere—there, one should approach a woman who has been observed through her gestures and facial expressions and whose intentions have been tested, provided she is alone. 3.4.35. For women whose intentions have been ascertained do not turn away when approached at the proper place and time, says Vātsyāyana. Thus end the approaches by a single man. (p. 221)

3.4.36. A girl who has an inferior reputation, even if she possesses good qualities, or one who is destitute of wealth, or though of noble birth, is not sought in marriage by her equals; or one who is separated from her parents, or lives with her paternal kinsmen, and has reached the age of puberty—such a girl may herself desire to take a husband. (p. 222) 3.4.37. She, however, should, out of affection for her son, entreat a man who is virtuous, capable, handsome, and pleasing to children. (p. 222)

3.4.38. Or, if he should think, "Even without the consent of his parents, this man might act toward me due to the weakness of his senses," she should win him over through agreeable and beneficial services and by frequenting his presence.
(p. 222) 3.4.39. And her mother, together with her female friends and nurses, should bring her face-to-face with him. (p. 223)
3.4.40. Approaching her when she has flowers, perfumes, and betel in her hand, or in a secluded place at an improper time;
or demonstrating skill in the arts, massaging, and pressing the head—these are the manifestations of propriety.
One should employ conversations suited to the man's temperament and act toward a young woman during the initial advances as previously described. (p. 223)
3.4.41. Furthermore, she should not herself initiate advances toward a man even in the interim;
for the teachers maintain that a young woman who initiates advances herself loses her good fortune. 3.4.42. However, when he has been prompted by her, one should accept his advances with compliance.
3.4.43. Even when embraced, she should not show any sign of transformation;
she should accept it as if unaware of his smooth gestures.
As for the seizing of her face, it is done by force.
3.4.44. When she is being solicited for the cultivation of sexual passion, the touching of the secret parts occurs only with difficulty.
3.4.45. Even when solicited, she should not reveal herself too openly, except at the time of the final decision.
3.4.46. But when he thinks, "He is devoted to me and will not turn away," then, while making his advances, he should urge him toward the release from his state of childhood.
3.4.47. And having been freed from her maidenhood, she should reveal it to those who are trustworthy. Thus ends the winning over of the man to be used. (p. 224)
3.4.48a. But a maiden being courted should take as her husband the one whom she considers a source of happiness; 3.4.48b. she should accept him who is well-disposed, submissive, and obedient.
3.4.49a. In a case where one disregards virtues, beauty, and even propriety...

3.4.49b. Out of greed for wealth, she might even act toward a husband who has rivals. 3.4.50ab. A maiden should not be seduced by a suitor who possesses the necessary qualities, is submissive, capable, powerful, and desirous, even while he employs various stratagems to win her over.

3.4.51 Even a poor man who is submissive, lacking in virtues, yet capable of supporting himself, is better than a husband who, though endowed with virtues, is shared by many. 3.4.52 Generally, the wives of wealthy men are numerous and unrestrained.
3.4.52b. Even when external enjoyment is available, those who lack confidence [in their own power] find pleasure only with outsiders.
3.4.53ab. A man who is base, or even one who is grey-haired, as well as one whose nature is to wander in foreign lands—such a person does not deserve union.
He who is prosecuted for a crime by mere chance, or even one primarily guilty of hypocrisy or gambling,
as well as he who has a co-wife or has offspring [from another man], does not deserve to enter into union [with the deceased].

3.4.55a. When there is equality of qualities among suitors, one suitor is preferable to another. 3.4.55b. In that case, the superiority of the suitor consists in his being characterized by affection. 3.5.1. Since it is generally impossible for a maiden to obtain a private audience, she should approach a foster-sister (*dhātreyikā*) after winning her over with things she likes and benefits her. (p. 227)

3.5.2. And she, remaining unrecognized by the hero, should win him over with his own virtues; she should describe the hero's qualities that are pleasing to her in the greatest detail. 3.5.3. She should point out the faults of other potential suitors' fathers as being contrary to his wishes.
3.5.4. Furthermore, she should point out the faults of her parents—such as their greed and fickleness—as well as the faults of her kinsmen.

3.5.5. She should also cite other maidens of similar birth, such as Śakuntalā and others, who, having obtained husbands through their own wit, lived happily; and she should show her examples of those who, even in great families, were oppressed by co-wives and became objects of hatred. 3.5.6. [She should show her] those who were being tormented by co-wives in noble lineages.

They are seen to be hated, suffering, and abandoned. (3.5.7) And he should describe the future prospects for him. (3.5.8) [He should describe] the unhindered happiness found in the solitary life of the heroine. (ch: nāyikā)
One should describe the passion of the hero;
and one should dispel, by means of appropriate reasons, the disappointment, anxiety, and shame of this woman whose desires are unfulfilled;
and one should perform the entire ritual of the female messenger (*dūtī*).
3.5.11. Thinking, "The hero will take her by force as if she were unaware," he should arrange matters so that she may be well-secured.

3.5.12. When she has consented and is staying in the desired place, the hero, having brought fire from the house of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), having spread *kuśa* grass, and having offered oblations according to tradition, should circumambulate [the fire] three times.
3.5.13. Thereafter, he should announce it to his mother and father.

3.5.14. "For marriages witnessed by the fire are not to be revoked," such is the established rule of the teachers. (p. 228) 3.5.15. Having defiled her, he should gradually make it known among his own kin.
3.5.16. He should manage the situation so that her relatives, seeking to avoid disgrace to their family and out of fear of punishment, shall give her back to him alone.
3.5.17. Immediately thereafter, he should gratify her kinsmen with affection and by winning their favor through passion.
3.5.18. Or he should proceed according to the Gāndharva form of marriage.

3.5.19. If she does not comply, he should win over another woman of the family who moves within the household, with whom she has had prior contact and who is well-disposed toward her; having secured her assistance, he should bring her to a secluded place under the pretext of some other business.
3.5.20. Then, [the ritual] beginning with "fire from the house of a Vedic scholar" is the same as previously described.
3.5.21. When the wedding is imminent, he should cause his mother to instill regret in her [the girl's] mother by pointing out faults that she herself finds objectionable.
3.5.22. Then, with her consent, having summoned the lover to the house of a neighbor at night, he should bring fire from the home of a learned Brahmin; the rest is the same as previously described.

3.5.23. Or, he should win over for a very long time her brother—whether he be of similar age or addicted to courtesans or the wives of others—by providing assistance in difficult undertakings and by winning his affection through pleasing favors.
At the end, he should cause him to accept his own purpose.
3.5.24. For generally, young men will even sacrifice their lives for the sake of companions who share their same character, vices, and age.
Therefore, she should have her brought by that very person under some other pretext.
Whether it is endurable or provides an opportunity is the same as previously stated. (p. 230)

3.5.25. On the eighth lunar day, during the moonlight, and on similar occasions, a nurse’s daughter, having caused her to drink an intoxicant under the pretext of some business of her own, should lead the heroine to a secluded place where the hero can approach her. There, having corrupted her while she is rendered unconscious by intoxication, [the procedure] is the same as described previously.

(p. 230) 3.5.26. When she is asleep, the nurse’s daughter, having kept her company alone, should corrupt her while she is unable to regain consciousness; [the procedure] is the same as described previously. (p. 230)
3.5.27. Having learned that she is going to another village or to a garden, the hero, well-prepared with his companions, should then abduct the maiden after terrifying or killing her guards.
These are the methods for marriage. (p. 231) 3.5.28a.
According to the established dharma, each preceding form of marriage is superior to the one following it. (p. 231)

3.5.28b. In the absence of the preceding, each subsequent one should be performed. 3.5.29ab. Since the fruit of marriages contracted by choice is mutual affection, even the middling Gāndharva marriage, being characterized by immediate union, is therefore honored.
3.5.30a. Because it is pleasant, involves little distress, and is free from obstacles in this world;
3.5.30b. and because its nature consists of mutual affection, the Gāndharva form is considered the most excellent.
4. [The section] concerning the wife.
4.1. The Conduct of the Wife Who Goes Out Alone and the Practice of Living Abroad.
4.1.1. A wife who goes out alone, maintaining secret confidence, should behave with favor toward her husband as if he were a god.
4.1.2. She should take upon herself the care of the household according to his will.

4.1.3. The dwelling should be clean, with well-swept areas, adorned with various flowers, its floor smooth, pleasing to the sight, where the ritual of offerings is performed at the three times of day, and where the shrines of the gods are honored. 4.1.4. For there is nothing else that so captivates the minds of householders as this, says Gonardīya.
4.1.5. One should show appropriate respect toward teachers, the circle of servants, the brothers-in-law, and their husbands.
4.1.6. When the fields have been cleared, one should cause green vegetable plots to be made, as well as clumps of sugarcane and thickets of cumin, mustard, ajamoda, śatapuṣpā, and tamāla.

4.1.7. In the grove of trees, one should establish level mounds for kubjaka, āmalaka, mallikā, jātī, kuraṇṭaka, navamālikā, tagara, nandyāvarta, japā, and other many-flowered shrubs, as well as bālaka, uśīraka, and pātālikā.
One should have pleasant things constructed.
(4.1.8) In the center, one should have a well, a pond, or a long tank excavated.
(4.1.9) One should not associate with female mendicants, Buddhist nuns, Jain ascetics, unchaste women, deceivers, fortune-tellers, or root-doctors.
4.1.10. Regarding food, she should discern: "This is to his liking," "this is disliked by him," "this is wholesome," and "this is unwholesome.

4.1.11. Having heard his voice from outside as he approaches the house, saying, "What is to be done? she should stand ready in the middle of the house. 4.1.12. Having dismissed the female attendant, she herself should wash his feet.

4.1.13. Furthermore, she should not remain in a secluded place in the sight of her husband with her ornaments removed. 4.1.14. If she should engage in excessive expenditure or improper spending, he should admonish her in private.
4.1.15. She may attend weddings, marriages, sacrifices, and social gatherings with her female friends, or visit temples, provided she has received permission to do so.
4.1.16. And in all amusements, she should engage in accordance with his inclinations.
4.1.17. She should go to bed after him, rise before him, and not wake him while he is sleeping. 4.1.18. The kitchen should be well-guarded and yet pleasant to look upon.
4.1.19. When her husband behaves improperly toward her, she should not become even slightly resentful, nor should she reproach him excessively.
4.1.20. However, she may reprimand him with words of censure when he is in the midst of his friends or when he is alone; yet she must never be the one who initiates a quarrel.

4.1.21. "For there is no other cause for lack of confidence than this," says Gonardīya. (p. 236) 4.1.22. One should avoid speaking ill, looking with ill-will, consulting with others, standing at the gateway, or peering in; likewise, one should avoid consulting in pleasure gardens or staying for a long time in secluded places.
(p. 236) 4.1.23. One should also become aware of the sweat, the stains on the teeth, and the foul odors [of the body], as these are causes for the loss of passion. (p. 237)
4.1.24. Abundant ornaments, various flowers and ointments, and garments radiant with diverse body-pastes constitute the attire for approaching [the king].

4.1.25. Wearing thin, smooth, and few fine silken cloths, limited jewelry, fragrance, and ointment that is not too intense, as well as white or other such flowers, constitutes the attire for recreation.
4.1.26. She should herself follow the husband’s observances and fasts by performing them as well;
and when she is forbidden [from something], she should desist from her speech, thinking, "I am not to be obstinate in this matter.
4.1.27. And at the proper time, she should purchase earthenware, articles made of split bamboo, wood, leather, and metal vessels while they are cheap.
4.1.28. Likewise, there shall be the secret storage within the residences of salt, fats, fragrant substances, pungent items, vessels, and medicinal herbs that are difficult to obtain.

4.1.29. And [the storage] of all medicinal plants, such as radish, yam, pālaṅkī, damanaka, āmrātaka, ervāruka, trapusa, vārtāka, kūṣmāṇḍa, alābu, sūraṇa, śukanāsā, svayaṃguptā, tilaparṇī, agnimantha, garlic, onion, and so forth.
She should attend to the gathering of seeds and their sowing at the proper time (4.1.30).

She should not disclose her own excellence to others, nor that which was discussed with her husband (4.1.31). And she should surpass her co-wives through her skill, brilliance, culinary art, dignity, and likewise through her refined conduct.
4.1.32. Having calculated the annual income, one should carry out expenditures corresponding to that amount.
4.1.33. From the milk remaining after consumption, one should produce clarified butter (*ghṛta*); likewise, [one should produce] oil and molasses.
Furthermore, [one should carry out] the spinning of cotton into thread and the weaving of that thread into cloth.
The gathering of carrying-ropes, cords, and bark;
the supervision of pounding, husking, and winnowing;
and [the collection of] rinsings, scum, husks, and broken grains.
The utilization of charcoal for brick-making;
knowledge of the maintenance of servants and their wages;
and the methods for the management of agriculture, cattle-rearing, and the yoking of draft animals.
One should know that this includes the observation of sheep, cocks, quails, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, peacocks, monkeys, and deer,
as well as the daily calculation of expenditures.

4.1.34. There shall be a store of worn-out garments for the lowest-ranking attendants; or, by those of various colors or even clean ones, there shall be a favor shown to the attendants who have performed their duties, as well as gifts for the sake of honor or for other uses.

4.1.35. There shall be the storage of jars of *surā* liquor and jars of *āsava* spirits, as well as their consumption, and the purchase and sale thereof, along with the supervision of income and expenditure.

4.1.36. One should honor the husband’s friends in accordance with propriety by giving them garlands, ointments, and betel. 4.1.37. One should attend upon the mother-in-law and father-in-law, remain dependent on them, avoid speaking with arrogance, keep one's speech measured and not harsh, laugh softly, and behave toward their likes and dislikes as if they were one's own.
4.1.38. Absence of arrogance regarding enjoyments.
4.1.39. Courtesy toward the retinue.
4.1.40. Giving nothing to anyone without first informing the leader.
4.1.41. Directing the servants in their respective duties and honoring him during festivals—this is the conduct of a woman who lives alone.

(p. 240) 4.1.42. When he is away on a journey, she should look after the household while wearing only auspicious ornaments, being devoted to the deities and fasting, and remaining intent on news of his welfare.
(p. 240) 4.1.43. And her bed shall be at the feet of her elders. (p. 240)
That is the accomplishment of desired tasks; and it is the exertion in acquiring and refining the objects desired by the leader. (p.
240) 4.1.44. Appropriate expenditure on obligatory and occasional rites.
She should have the intention of completing the tasks she has begun.

(4.1.45) She should not visit her family circle except on occasions of misfortune or festivals; even then, she should not remain there for too long and must not be attended by her husband’s retinue, nor should she wear the dress appropriate for travel. (4.1.46)
4.1.46. For those permitted by their elders, there shall be the performance of fasts.

With pure attendants supervised by authorized officials, the replenishment of resources shall be carried out through transactions of purchase and sale as approved, along with the reduction of expenditures according to one's capacity.

(p. 241) 4.1.47. Upon his return, she should first see him while he remains in his natural state; then follows the worship of the deities and the bringing of offerings—this constitutes the conduct regarding travel abroad.
And you have two verses on this point:
A woman who desires the welfare of her husband should follow his virtuous conduct—whether she be a woman of noble family, a remarried woman, a courtesan, or even one who wanders alone. (4.1.48)

4.1.49ab. Women who have resorted to virtuous conduct obtain dharma, as well as wealth, pleasure, and high status; (p.242) 4.1.49cd. And they obtain a husband free from rivals and endowed with good character. (p.242) 4.2.1. A husband may take a second wife due to the stupidity, misconduct, or misfortune of his first wife, from the failure to produce offspring, from the repeated birth of daughters, or from the fickleness of the husband. (p.242)
4.2.2. At that time, from the very beginning, she should seek to win them over by demonstrating her devotion, virtuous character, and cleverness;
and when children are born, she herself should incite rivalry among the co-wives.
4.2.3. And while she is being superseded [by a rival], she should, to the best of her ability, cause herself to be established as superior.
4.2.4. When she has arrived, he should look upon her as a sister.
With great care, he should have her perform the evening rite known to the leader; yet he should pay no heed to any change in her demeanor arising from her good fortune or to her arrogance.
4.2.5. He should overlook her if she becomes negligent toward her husband.
Where she might think, "She will understand this matter for herself," there he should instruct her with great care.
(4.2.6) And in private, within the hearing of the hero, he should show her further special details.
(4.2.7) There is no distinction regarding his children.
Excessive compassion toward the circle of attendants, affection toward the circle of friends,
and a lack of excessive regard for one's own kinsmen.
And she should show great zeal toward his kinsmen.

(4.2.8) However, if she has been superseded by many [wives], she should associate with one who is not separated from her [by rank]. (4.2.9) But whichever woman the husband desires to favor, she should incite a quarrel between them by praising that woman as having previously been fortunate. (4.2.9)
4.2.11. Among them, the wicked woman (*durjanī*), remaining herself free from dispute, should cause that woman whom she intends to win over through her unity to become estranged.
4.2.12. But when she has been quarreled with by the hero, the [wicked woman] should console her, bolstering her with the support of partiality. 4.2.13. And she should further increase the quarrel.
4.2.14. Or, having perceived a slight quarrel, she herself should inflame it further.

(p.245) 4.2.15. If she thinks that the husband is still conciliatory toward her even today, then she herself should strive for a reconciliation; such is the conduct of the senior wife (*jyeṣṭhā*). (p.245) 4.2.16. But the junior wife (*kaniṣṭhā*) should regard her co-wife as a mother. (p.245)
4.2.17. She should not use even her share of the paternal inheritance without his knowledge. 4.2.18. She should manage those [assets] for her own livelihood under his supervision.
4.2.19. Having obtained his permission, she may lie with her husband.
4.2.20. Nor indeed should she report her husband's words to another woman.
4.2.21. She should regard his offspring as more important than her own. 4.2.22. She should serve her husband with special care in private.
4.2.23. She should not speak of the suffering arising from the transformation of her co-wife caused by herself.
4.2.24. She should seek a special, secret mark of respect from her husband.
4.2.25. She should say, "Indeed, it is by this giving of wholesome food that I live."
4.2.26. However, she should not speak of it outside [the household] out of pride or passion. 4.2.27. For one whose secrets are disclosed incurs the contempt of her husband.
4.2.28. Gonardīya says that, out of fear of her elder sister-in-law, she should remain one who desires honor while keeping it concealed.

4.2.29. One should show compassion toward an elder sister who is unfortunate or childless, and she should likewise show compassion toward her husband. 4.2.30. However, if she acts by force, she should follow the conduct of one who lives alone; this is the conduct of a younger sister. 4.2.31. But a widow who, due to weakness of the senses, being afflicted, marries again a man who possesses wealth and good qualities, she is a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman).

4.2.32. But when she departs again of her own free will, [the husband] should consider that "she is devoid of virtue" and then seek another; so say the followers of Bābhravya. (p.247) 4.2.33. She, it is said, being a seeker of pleasure, may indeed find another. (p.247) 4.2.34.
Gonardīya maintains that since there is a totality of pleasure in the enjoyment of virtues, she is therefore superior to the former case. (p.247)
4.2.35. "From her own inclination toward his mind," says Vātsyāyana.

(p.248) 4.2.36. She should seek from her kinsmen through the suitor such activities as supporting expenses for drinking parties, garden excursions, religious festivals, gifts, and the honoring of friends.
(p.248) 4.2.37. Or, according to her own means, she should wear his ornaments or her own. (p.248)

He should enter his house as if he were a powerful lord. (4.2.41) But he should behave with affection toward women of noble birth.
(4.2.42) He should treat the household servants with courtesy, and his conduct toward friends should be accompanied by friendly jesting.
She should possess skill in the arts (kalās) and superior knowledge.
(4.2.43) / In occasions of quarrel, she herself should reproach the hero.
(4.2.44) / And in private, she should attend to him with the sixty-four arts.
She should personally assist her co-wives and give them ornaments for their children, treating those children as if they were her own.
One should behave as toward a master; one should carefully prepare ornaments and attire;
and one should give more abundant gifts to the servants and the circle of friends.
Frequenting social gatherings, drinking parties, garden excursions, and pleasure parks—this is the conduct of a remarried woman (punarbhu).
(4.2.45) But as for an unfortunate woman who is oppressed by her co-wives, she should seek refuge with one among them who treats her with particular kindness toward the husband.
[The following points] are to be made public: [...]
She should demonstrate her proficiency in the various arts and sciences;
due to her lack of ill fortune, there shall be no concealment of secrets.
(4.2.46) She should act as a foster-mother to the children of the hero. (p. 250)
4.2.47. Having won over her friends, she should demonstrate her own devotion through them.
4.2.48. She should be one who precedes him in religious duties, as well as in vows and fasts.
4.2.49. She should show courtesy toward the household servants.
And she should not regard herself as superior.
(4.2.50) On the bed, she should win back his affection through familiarity with him.
(4.2.51) She should neither reproach him nor display perversity.
4.2.52. And she with whom he has quarreled, he may, if he so desires, win her back.
4.2.53. And whichever woman he desires in secret, he should bring her together with him and keep her concealed.
4.2.54. He should take such measures that the man-about-town believes her to be devoted to her husband and free from deceit; this is the conduct of an unfortunate woman.
4.2.55. One should observe the conduct of the women of the harem within these very same sections.
4.2.56. The chamberlains or the senior ladies-in-waiting should present to the king the garlands, ointments, and garments for those women, saying, "These were sent by the queens.
4.2.57. Having received them, the king should give back to them the used garlands as a return gift.
4.2.58. Adorned himself, he should, in the afternoon, view all the women of the inner apartments together with their own ornaments. 4.2.59.
He should attend to their proper places and honors according to the time and their respective status, and engage them in conversations accompanied by gentle jests. 4.2.60.
Immediately after that, he should likewise visit the *punarbhu* (women who have been remarried).
4.2.61. Beyond that are the courtesans (*veśyā*), those of the inner apartments (*ābhyantarikā*), and those of the theater (*nāṭakīyā*).
4.2.62. Their respective locations are in the courtyards (*kakṣā*) as previously described.

4.2.63. The wardens of the quarters (*vāsaka-pālī*), however, attend upon her whose residence is current, her whose has passed, and her who is in her fertile season (*ṛtu*), accompanied by their female attendants.

When the king has risen from his daytime rest, they should present him with the unguents sent by those two, marked with their signet rings, as well as inform him of the season and the designated quarters.
(4.2.64) In that regard, whichever woman the king takes hold of, he shall order her to be his exclusive consort (*vāsaka*).
4.2.65. During festivals, all [the women] shall receive worship according to their rank, as well as drinking parties and performances of music. (p.
252) 4.2.66. For those who move within the inner apartments, there is no going outside; for outsiders, there is no entry.
Except for those whose purity is well-known;
and the application of ritual action must not be impaired—this is the rule regarding the women of the inner apartments.
And there are verses on this point:
"A man, having taken many wives, should be equal toward them;
he should not practice contempt for them, nor should he tolerate their offenses."

4.2.68ab. Whatever amorous play or bodily transformation occurs with one woman, 4.2.68cd. Or whatever reproach arises from confidence—she should not mention that to others. 4.2.69ab. She should never give any opportunity to women for the sake of her co-wife.

4.2.69cd. Likewise, he should apply those very same faults to her when she reproaches him. 4.2.70ab. He should please one woman with confidential intimacies in private, another with public honors, and yet another with marks of high esteem; in this manner, he should win over women.

4.2.71ab. By means of excursions to gardens, enjoyments, gifts, and the honoring of her kinsmen; (p.254) 4.2.71cd. And by secret amorous unions, he should thus gratify each one individually. (p.254) 4.2.72ab. A young woman who has conquered anger and acts according to the scriptures... (p.254)

4.2.72cd / She brings her husband under her control and overcomes her co-wives. 5. Adultery: 5.1. The establishment of the character of women and men; the causes for turning [them away from misconduct]; men are easily accomplished among women, while women are won without effort.
5.1.2. Among these, one should examine from the very outset whether the object is achievable, free from danger, accessible, and what its future course and maintenance will be.
5.1.3. But when he sees [the soul] moving at will from one station to another, he may accept the possessions of others for the sake of protecting his own body from injury.
5.1.4. There are, however, ten stages of desire (kāma).

5.1.5. They are: delight of the eye, attachment of the mind, the arising of volition, loss of sleep, emaciation, withdrawal from sense objects, loss of shame, madness, fainting, and death. These are their [stages].
5.1.6. Regarding this, the teachers maintain that one should observe a young woman’s character, truthfulness, purity, tractability, and impetuousness through her physical form and bodily marks.
5.1.7. Vātsyāyana, however, holds that because physical forms and marks can be deceptive, the actual disposition of a woman must be understood solely through her gestures and facial expressions.
5.1.8. Upon seeing any man who is radiant, a woman falls in love with him.
In the same way, a man also [does not act] toward a woman;
however, Goṇikāputra maintains that he does not fail to act because of mutual dependence.
5.1.9. In this regard, there is a distinction concerning women.
(p. 257) 5.1.10. A woman does not consider what is dharma and what is adharma; she simply desires.
However, out of consideration for her duty, she does not initiate a sexual advance.
5.1.11. Furthermore, due to her own nature, even when being courted by a man, she may turn away despite desiring to act.
5.1.12. Yet, when courted again and again, she succeeds.
5.1.13. A man, however, even while desiring her, may turn away out of regard for the stability of dharma and the conventions of the noble.
5.1.14. Likewise, one who lacks intelligence does not achieve success even when applying himself. 5.1.15. He applies himself without cause;
and having applied himself, he does not apply himself again.
And when she has been won, he falls into indifference;
it is a common saying that "one despises what is easily obtained and longs for what is difficult to obtain. (p. 257)
5.1.17. In that regard, the causes for turning away [from the practice] are as follows:
5.1.22. Perceiving [the teacher] as being separated [from his disciples];
5.1.23. Anger arising from the thought, "He addresses me with contempt."
5.1.24. "It is beyond reasoning" refers to the abandonment of mental constructs (*saṃkalpa*).
5.1.25. "He will go," "there is no future [certainty]," and "his mind is attached elsewhere.
5.1.26. "His outward appearance is unrestrained" refers to agitation (*uddvega*).
5.1.27. "He has entrusted his heart to his friends"—this implies concern for them.
5.1.29. "He is spirited"—this causes apprehension. 5.1.30. "He is of fierce impetuosity or possesses a noble chariot"—this inspires fear in the doe.

5.1.31. "The citizen is skilled in the arts"—this is a cause for shame. 5.1.32. "He has been treated as a friend"—and this too. 5.1.33. "He does not know the proper place and time"—this is a cause for resentment.
5.1.34. To be treated with contempt means to lack respect. 5.1.35. Not to take notice even when summoned is disdain.
5.1.36. And for the female elephant, [to say] "the hare has slow speed" [is an insult].
5.1.37. Compassion (*anukampā*) is the thought: "May no undesirable thing happen to him because of me.
5.1.38. Disgust (*nirveda*) arises from perceiving faults within oneself.
5.1.39. Fear (*bhaya*) is the thought: "Once she is known [to be unchaste], I shall be cast out by my own kin."
5.1.40. "Grey-haired" is a term of disrespect. 5.1.41. "Examined by his master" refers to deliberation.
5.1.43. Whatever one perceives within oneself regarding these [qualities], one should determine that from the very beginning. (p. 259)
5.1.44. Those [faults] associated with nobility arise from the increase of passion.
5.1.45. Those born of incapacity arise from the failure to demonstrate the proper means.
5.1.46. Those caused by excessive honor arise from over-familiarity.
5.1.47. [One should pacify] those [actions] caused by humiliation through great heroism and discernment;
5.1.48. those born of such humiliation through prostration;
5.1.49. those joined with fear through reassurance. (p. 260)

5.1.50. These men are generally successful: one who knows the *Kāmasūtra*; one skilled in storytelling and narration; one who has been associated with her since childhood; one whose youth is fully developed; one who has gained her confidence through play and other activities;
one who performs her errands; one who speaks appropriately; one who does what is pleasing; one who was previously her messenger; and one who knows her secrets.
He was secretly solicited by his friend Uttamā; he was a neighbor who grew up together with her, renowned for his good fortune,
devoted to pleasure,
and likewise served as an attendant under the care of Dhātreyikā.

A man who is a new bridegroom, fond of spectacles and gardens, generous by nature, a bull among men, one whose prowess is proven, daring, and heroic—one who surpasses her husband in learning, beauty, virtues, and enjoyments, and who possesses costly dress and refined manners—[is a type of man].
(5.1.51) Just as a man perceives his own success [with a woman], so too should he perceive that of women.
(5.1.52) However, these women are easily won without effort; they are won merely by an advance.
Standing at the gateway,
looking out from the palace toward the royal road,
she joined in social gatherings at the houses of her young neighbors.
Constantly watching;
having been watched while looking to the side;
and being superseded by a co-wife without cause.
She hates her husband and is disliked by him; she is devoid of protection; she is childless;
or her children have perished.
One who joins social gatherings; one who joins in affection;
the wife of an actor.
A young woman whose husband has died; a poor woman who possesses many articles of enjoyment;
an elder wife who has many brothers-in-law.
One who is conceited yet has a husband of inferior status;
one who prides herself on her skill but is distressed by her husband’s stupidity;
or one who, due to a lack of discrimination, is tormented by greed.

5.1.54. She was sought with great effort during her maidenhood, yet she was not obtained by him at that time; she is of equal intellect, character, wisdom, understanding, and temperament. She is naturally partial [to him], yet she has been insulted despite having committed no offense.

And she was surpassed by women of equal form who were wives of men away from home; and [she was surpassed by those whose husbands were] jealous, foul-smelling, fastidious, impotent, procrastinating, base, humpbacked, dwarf, deformed, jewel-makers, rustic, ill-smelling, diseased, or old.
There are two verses on this point:
5.1.55ab. Desire arises from its own nature and is nourished by action.
5.1.55cd. Purified by the intellect and free from agitation, she becomes steady and unswerving.
5.1.56ab. Having recognized his own success and inferred the signs of women, 5.1.56cd. the man who eliminates the causes for turning away succeeds with women.
5.2. Causes for Acquaintance and Approaches (Abhiyoga).

5.2.1. Just as a maiden is won by one's own direct approach (*abhiyoga*), she is not so easily won through a female messenger (*dūtī*); however, the wives of others, possessing subtle dispositions, are won through a messenger and not so much by oneself—so say the teachers (p. 265).

5.2.2. Vātsyāyana maintains that in all cases where one possesses the necessary capability, it is more appropriate to act as one's own intermediary (*svayaṃ sādhana*), because employing a female messenger (*dūtī*) is difficult to accomplish. 5.2.3. It is the general consensus that those who are impulsive for the first time and those whose conversation is unrestrained should be won over by oneself; whereas those of the opposite character should generally be approached through a messenger.

5.2.4. But one who intends to make an advance himself should first establish a familiarity [with her]. (p. 265) 5.2.5. Her appearance may be either natural or intentional. 5.2.6. The natural occurs when he is in the vicinity of his own residence; the intentional occurs when he is in the vicinity of the residences of friends, kinsmen, high officials, or physicians, or on occasions such as weddings, sacrifices, festivals, calamities, or visits to parks. (p. 266)
5.2.7 And when she is visible, there is constant gazing at her with all her features, arranging her hair, clipping her nails,
adorning herself with ornaments, rubbing her lower lip, and various playful gestures while watching her together with her female companions;
as well as conversations related to him under some other pretext, and the manifestation of both renunciation and enjoyment while sitting on the lap of a friend.
Yawning with a stretching of the limbs; raising one eyebrow; speaking softly; listening to her words;
engaging in a conversation with another person, whether a child or an adult, that is directed toward her and possesses a double meaning; personally expressing one's desire for her under some pretext;
kissing and embracing her while using a child as a pretext; and giving her betel-leaf with one's own tongue.
The touching of the region of the jaw with the forefinger should be applied in that manner, according to what is appropriate and as occasion allows.

Furthermore, one should fondle the child who has come into one's lap, give him children’s toys and take them back from him because of his proximity, engage him in conversation, and, having gained the affection of those capable of conversing with him, [proceed accordingly]. 5.2.8.
The purpose, its consequences, the arrangement for going and not going, and her reliance [on him]— for one who does not perceive these,
what indeed is the talk of the *Kāmasūtra*?
(5.2.9) But when intimacy has developed, one should place a trust or a deposit in her hand.
He should take from her daily and at every moment small portions of *saugandhika* and betel nuts (5.2.10).
He should engage her in confidential conversation with his own wives and in private seating.
5.2.11. [This is] for the purpose of constant sight and for the purpose of gaining confidence.

5.2.12. Among goldsmiths, jewelers, lapidaries, dyers of indigo and safflower, and so forth, she who desires pleasure should herself strive to accomplish it with those who are under her control, together with them.
5.2.13. For one intent upon that practice, there is a long-term association of constant sight known to the world.
5.2.14. And in that regard, there is also the consideration of other activities.

5.2.15. She should demonstrate as being within her own power the application, the production, the source, the means, and the specialized knowledge of whatever activity, material, or skill she may require.
5.2.16. She should engage in debate with her attendants and with her family circle regarding worldly practices previously undertaken and regarding the examination of the qualities of materials.
5.2.17. In that regard, he should employ her as an arbiter among those who have been designated as negotiators.

5.2.18. But when she disputes with him, he should say, "It is absolutely true. These are the means for gaining familiarity. 5.2.19. Once she has become familiar and has revealed her gestures and expressions, he should approach her by means of stratagems, as one would a maiden.
Generally, in that case, the applications should be subtle,
because girls have not yet engaged in sexual union; in the case of other women, one should apply those very same methods more openly.
Because of their association [with him].
5.2.20. When she has displayed her charms, revealed her true nature, and engaged in the act of enjoyment, one should employ his [belongings] for that purpose.
5.2.21. In this regard, one should use his own highly precious perfumes, upper garment (*uttarīya*), and flowers.
There may also be a finger-ring.
Below that, while she holds betel in her hand, she requests flowers from the hair-braids of one who is intent on going to a social gathering.
In that situation, she should give him highly precious, desirable perfume, marked with the impressions of her own nails and teeth, along with significant gestures.
5.2.23. By means of increasingly intense advances, one should dispel her timidity.

(p. 269) 5.2.24. Gradually, in a secluded place, there should be going toward her, embracing, kissing, taking and giving betel, the exchange of articles at the conclusion of the gift-giving, and touching the private parts.
5.2.25. And where she is already occupied by one [man], one should not make advances toward another there.
In that regard, one should win over those who have experienced objects of pleasure when old by means of affectionate conciliations.
There are two verses on this point:
5.2.27ab. Wherever the hero—the husband of that woman—is seen to have frequent access elsewhere, 5.2.27cd. there he should not approach any woman, even one who is easily accessible.
5.2.28ab. A wise man, knowing his own competence, should not make advances toward a woman who is suspicious, guarded, frightened, or under the watchful eye of her mother-in-law.
(p. 270) 5.3. Examination of Disposition (*bhāvaparīkṣā*)
5.3.1. One who makes advances toward women should examine their conduct; through that, her disposition is tested. He should also accept her advances. (p. 271)
5.3.2. One should accomplish this woman by means of a messenger who does not disclose the mantra.
5.3.3. One should recognize her as being divided in mind when she does not accept the suitor's advances yet continues to associate with him;
one should accomplish her gradually.

5.3.4. If she does not accept his advances, but appears again adorned with special finery and approaches him in private just as before, one should know her to be capable of being won by force. 5.3.5. She who endures even many advances and yet does not surrender herself even after a long time is one who accepts [love] only when it is dry (i.e., insincere); she is to be won by breaking off her acquaintance. 5.3.7. Even when approached, she avoids him.
He neither mixes with them nor rejects them,
because of his sense of respect and self-importance toward that [other] self.
Through excessive familiarity, she becomes difficult to win over;
one should win her over by means of a female messenger who knows the vital points (*marmajñā*).
(5.3.8) If, when being courted, she rejects him with harshness, he should disregard her.
5.3.9. Even after having treated her harshly, one should win over the woman who is inclined toward affection.
5.3.10. She endures physical contact for a specific reason but does not truly understand it; with a divided mind, she is to be won over either through constant patience or by means of persistence.
5.3.11. While she is lying nearby, he should pretend to sleep and place his hand upon her.
She too remains indifferent as if asleep;
however, being awake and desiring further union, she should repel him again.
(5.3.12) By this, the practice of placing one foot upon the other has been explained. (p. 273)
5.3.13. When that [intercourse] has been completed, one should again employ the method of embracing while she is asleep.
5.3.14. One should recognize her as being in her natural state, desiring union, and having risen on the second day if she was unable to endure it;
however, if she does not appear at all, she is to be won over by means of a female messenger (dūtī).
5.3.15. Even if she has not been seen for a long time, she remains in her natural state; once she has manifested her characteristics and displayed her form, one should approach her.
5.3.16. Though she may not be actively seeking him, she signals her interest;
and in a secluded place, she reveals herself.
She speaks with a faltering voice;
her fingers, hands, and feet become perspired, as does her face.
When there is a headache or a need for massaging, she directs herself toward the thighs of the hero.
5.3.17. A woman who is ill or a masseuse, while massaging with one hand, indicates her touch and embraces him with her second arm;
she acts with an air of feigned astonishment.
5.3.18. Or, as if blinded by sleep, she remains touching him with both her thighs and her arms.
She causes one part after another to fall upon his thighs; intent on massaging the roots of his thighs, she does not move against the grain,
but places one hand right there, motionless.
And having squeezed him with a limb-grip, she releases him only after a long time.
(5.3.19) Having thus accepted the advances of the lover, she approaches him again on the second day for the purpose of massaging;
yet she does not engage in excessive physical contact. (5.3.20)
And she does not avoid him.
5.3.21. She displays her affection in a secluded place, openly and without cause, except in a hidden location.

5.3.22. If she is one who can be enjoyed by a nearby attendant, and even when summoned behaves in that same manner, she is to be won over by a female messenger who knows her vital points (*marmajñā*).
"But when she turns away, she must be investigated"—this is the examination of the internal state.
And there are verses on this point:
First one should cultivate familiarity, and then engage in conversation;
mixed with conversation, there should be a mutual discernment of outward signs.
5.3.25ab. If he perceives through her reply the manifestation of her internal state, 5.3.25cd. then the man, free from hesitation, should make his advances toward the woman.
5.3.26ab. That woman who first reveals her own disposition through her outward expression...

5.3.26cd. She should be approached immediately, indeed at the very first sight. 5.3.27ab. But she who, when gently summoned, gives a clear response, 5.3.27cd. she too should be known as one intent on pleasure, accomplished at that very moment.

5.3.28ab. In the case of a woman who is steady, of long-standing practice, bold, and experienced, this subtle method has been declared; for such women are clearly those who have already attained success. (p.276) 5.4. The Duties of the Female Messenger (dūtī).
5.4.1. When she has displayed her gestures and facial expressions, but is seen only rarely and is [otherwise] unknown, one should approach her through a female messenger.

5.4.2. Having gained access to her through her character, the messenger should win her over by means of stories under the guise of tales, methods for making oneself beloved, accounts of worldly conduct, the narratives of poets, stories concerning those who have wives of others, and by praising her beauty, discernment, courtesy, and virtuous nature.
5.4.3. How might she cause him to feel regret, thinking, "How can such a man as this be your husband?
5.4.4. She should say, "O fortunate lady, it is not even fit for you to serve him.

5.4.5. She should point out his lack of passion, jealousy, deceitfulness, ingratitude, lack of sexual interest, miserliness, fickleness, and whatever other hidden faults he possesses that come to light when she is near him.
One should speak with excellence regarding what is truly existent.
Furthermore, by whatever fault one perceives her to be distressed, one should enter [her confidence] through that very same means. 5.4.6.
5.4.7. When she is a doe, there is no fault in her being a [non-human] rabbit. 5.4.8. By this very same principle, the cases of the mare and the female elephant are also explained. (p.277) 5.4.9.

However, Goṇikāputra maintains that one should approach a woman as a messenger only after having gained her confidence, specifically in the case of a woman who has committed her first transgression or one whose feelings are subtle. (p.277)

5.4.10. She should recount the conduct, the compliance, and the desires of the suitor. 5.4.11. When her sincere affection has been manifested, she should skillfully speak thus regarding the body of the matter:
5.4.12. "Listen to this wonderful thing, O fortunate lady."
"Indeed, having seen you there, this leader, the son of such-and-such a clan, is suffering from a derangement of mind;
for he is by nature delicate, and this poor man has never before been afflicted elsewhere. Therefore, it is now possible that he might even experience death," so she would describe.
5.4.13. There, having observed signs of success on the second day—namely, serenity in her speech, her face, and her gaze—he should again initiate conversation.
5.4.14. While she listens, he should tell stories such as those of Ahalyā, Avimāraka, and Śakuntalā, as well as other worldly tales appropriate to the occasion.
5.4.15. He should describe the hero's virility, his mastery of the sixty-four arts, and his good fortune.
One should describe his praiseworthy nature and his secret association, whether it be real or previously unreal;
and one should observe her outward appearance. 5.4.16. (p.278)
