5.4.17. Having seen her smiling, he addresses her.
5.4.18. And he invites her to sit on a seat.
5.4.19. "Where have you been staying? Where have you slept? Where..."
She asks, "Where was food eaten, what was done, or what was performed? (5.4.20).
She reveals herself in a secluded place (5.4.21).
She assigns him narrative tales.
5.4.22. Thinking of him, she sighs and yawns;
5.4.23. she gives gifts out of affection;
5.4.24. and she remembers him during desired festivals.
5.4.25. She dismisses him while maintaining a connection for a future meeting.
5.4.26. Being a speaker of what is right, she persists in the conversation, saying, "Why do you speak such an unseemly thing?
5.4.27. She points out the hero's faults related to his deceitfulness and fickleness.

5.4.28. She does not herself mention a previous meeting or an application of conversation that had occurred before, yet she listens with interest when such things are mentioned by her [female friend]. 5.4.29. When the hero's desires are being described, she laughs as if with derision, yet she does not speak out [her contempt]. (p. 279)
5.4.30. Through the female messenger, he should reinforce her—once her disposition has been revealed—by means of tokens known to the hero.
5.4.31. But if she is a stranger, he should win her over by recounting his virtues and stories of his passion.
5.4.32. Auddālaki maintains that there can be no role for a female messenger between two people who are strangers and have not seen one another's dispositions.
5.4.33. "It exists even between two who have not been previously acquainted, provided they appear to be intimate," so say the followers of Bābhravya.
5.4.34. "It exists even between two who are already acquainted, provided they do not appear to be intimate," so says Goṇikāputra.
5.4.35. "It exists even between two who are unacquainted and whose intimacy has not been seen, through the mediation of a female messenger," so says Vātsyāyana. (p. 281)
5.4.36. He should show her charming gifts sent by him—betel, ointment, a garland, a finger-ring, or a garment.
5.4.37. On these items, there should be nail-marks, tooth-prints, and various other signs of the hero, as appropriate.
5.4.38. And he should place a folded palm-mark (añjali) made with saffron upon the garment.

5.4.39. One should display leaf-cuttings (*pattra-chedya*) of various designs according to one's intention, as well as ear-leaf ornaments (*karṇa-pattra*) and floral crests (*āpīḍa*) containing written messages. 5.4.40. Through these, one should communicate one's own desires.
And she should be employed in the giving of reciprocal gifts.
(5.4.41) Thus, when mutual acceptance has been established, their union occurs through the mediation of a female messenger.
(5.4.42) That [union] may take place at a visit to a deity, on a journey, during garden sports, upon descending into water, at a wedding, at a sacrifice, or at festivals and calamities.
"In the event of a fire, during a disturbance caused by thieves, when the populace mounts a vehicle, and at various spectacles and public functions—so say the followers of Bābhravya.
'In the dwellings of female friends, Buddhist nuns, Jain ascetics, and female ascetics, it is an easy means [of access],' says Goṇikāputra. (5.4.43)

5.4.44. But Vātsyāyana maintains that entry into the house of that very woman—where the times of exit and entry are known, where remedies for anticipated misfortunes have been considered, where the exit is appropriate and the time of entry remains unknown—is a constant and easy means of pleasure.

5.4.45. The specific types of female messengers (*dūtī*) are: the one with full authority (*nisṛṣṭārthā*), the one with limited authority (*parimitārthā*), the bearer of a letter (*patrahārī*), the self-appointed messenger (*svayaṃdūtī*), the foolish messenger (*mūḍhadūtī*), the wife-messenger (*bhāryādūtī*), the mute messenger (*mūkadūtī*), and the wind-messenger (*vātadūtī*).
5.4.46. She who, having understood the purpose of the hero and the heroine as desired, accomplishes the task through her own intelligence, is the *nisṛṣṭārthā* (one with full authority).
5.4.47. She is generally [employed] by the heroine when they are already acquainted and have conversed.
5.4.48. When employed by the heroine, she may also act even when they are not yet acquainted and have not conversed.
5.4.49. And because of mutual curiosity, these two are suitable and appropriate for one another, even though they are strangers to each other.

5.4.50. Having perceived a portion of the task and a portion of the application, she brings the remainder to completion; thus, it is "one whose purpose is limited. 5.4.51. That [love] occurs when the mutual signs have been seen, but their sightings are infrequent.
5.4.52. One who conveys only a message is a letter-carrier (*patrahārī*).
(p. 284) 5.4.53. She [the letter-carrier] is employed for the purpose of addressing [the hero] regarding place and time when [the two lovers] are deeply in love and already united.
(p. 284) 5.4.54. Sent by another woman as a messenger, she should approach the hero herself, pretending not to know him; or she may describe her enjoyment with him in a dream.
He should criticize his wife’s lapses regarding her lineage and reproach her; under that pretext, he should himself display jealousy,
or perhaps give her something marked with nail or tooth impressions.

She should say, "I was intended by you to be given [to you] first," and she should inquire in private, "What pleasure do you find in my wife? She herself is the messenger (dūtī). Her meeting with him in private and her receiving gifts from him [constitute her role]. 5.4.55.

5.4.56. Under the pretext of accepting a gift, having lured another woman away, she should win over the hero by means of conveying messages to her, and then ruin that woman; she too is a "self-messenger" (svayaṃ-dūtī). 5.4.57. By this [method], the hero and other messengers are also explained. 5.4.58. Having gained the confidence of the hero’s innocent wife and entered her presence without restraint, she should inquire about the hero’s activities.
One should train her in the yogas;
one should adorn her with the ritual forms; one should cause her to grasp this wrathful [deity].
And one should cause her to hear: "Practice in this manner.
Furthermore, one should personally leave marks of fingernails and teeth upon her.
By means of that, she should summon the leader; she is the "foolish messenger" (mūḍhadūtī).
5.4.59. He should employ replies to her using that very same [strategy].
5.4.60. Or, having employed his own wife who is foolish, and having established confidence between her and [the woman], he should cause her to be summoned by that [wife] alone;
and he should manifest his own cleverness.
That wife is the messenger;
by her alone is the apprehension of her [the intended woman's] appearance achieved.
(5.4.61) Or, one should send a young female attendant who does not recognize faults, using a blameless means.
In that regard, when she places a secret letter, a nail-mark, or a tooth-print upon a garland or an ear-ornament, she is a silent messenger (*mūkadūtī*);
her request for a reply is made by means of that very same [token].

(5.4.62) She who, remaining indifferent, causes another person to overhear a statement that is connected with signs related to a previously introduced subject, which is unintelligible to others, and which possesses either a worldly meaning or a double meaning, is a messenger of the wind (*vātadūtī*).
Her request for a reply is likewise made by that very same [means]; such are their specific characteristics.
And there are verses on this subject:
A widow, a female fortune-teller, a female slave, a female mendicant, or a woman skilled in the arts—
such a woman quickly gains confidence and finds employment as a female messenger.
5.4.64ab. She should cause her to feel enmity toward her husband and describe [other men] as being full of charm.
5.4.64cd. She should also show her the various delights of sexual union experienced by other women. 5.4.65ab. Furthermore, she should point out the lover's passion and his skill in the arts of love.
5.4.65cd. And she should describe his entreaties to the superior women and his persistence.
5.4.66ab. Even an object not previously intended, once abandoned for reasons of some fault, 5.4.66cd.
the female messenger brings back again through her skill in speech.
5.5. The Will of the Lord (Īśvarakāmita).
5.5.1. It is not permitted for kings or high ministers to enter the houses of others;
for their conduct is observed by the great multitude and emulated by them. (p. 288)
5.5.2. The three worlds behold the rising sun and rise after it;
they also behold it as it goes and follow after it in its setting.
(p.288) 5.5.3. Therefore, because it is impossible [to do otherwise] and because it would be censurable, they would not perform anything in vain. (p.288)
5.5.4. However, when [sexual intercourse] must necessarily be practiced, one should employ the following methods.
5.5.5. For a village headman, an official, or the son of a plowman who is young, the women of the village can be won over by mere words;
these are called *carṣaṇīs* by the *viṭas*.
5.5.6. Together with them, there shall be their employment in forced labor; in the entry of goods into the storehouse and their removal or entry from it;
in the repair of buildings; in agricultural work; in the gathering of cotton, wool, flax, hemp, and bark-fiber; in the receiving of thread;
and in the purchase, sale, and barter of commodities, as well as in various other such tasks.
5.5.7. Likewise, [the superintendent of cows] with the women of Vraja; (p.290) 5.5.8.
[The superintendent of threads] with widows, those without protectors, and female ascetics; (p.290) 5.5.9.
[The superintendent of the city] with those who flirt while wandering at night, because they know his vulnerable points. (p.290)

5.5.11. On occasions such as the eighth-day moon, the Kaumudī festival, and the beautiful spring, the women of the towns, cities, and market-towns generally engage in play within the palace of the lord together with the ladies of the harem.
5.5.12. And there, at the conclusion of the drinking bouts, the city women, according to their acquaintance, [approach] the ladies of the harem individually.
Having entered separately into the pleasure-houses and dwellings, and having sat with them while conversing, being honored and well-satisfied, they should depart at the approach of evening.
There, a female servant of the king previously acquainted with the woman to be employed should converse with her.

5.5.14. She should engage her in viewing beautiful sights. 5.5.15. Even before she has reached her own quarters, he should say: "In this pleasure-garden, I shall show you the beautiful sights of the royal palace," and he should arrange for them at the appropriate time.
"Outside, I shall show you the floor of coral sprouts;

the jeweled ground; the orchard; the vine-pavilion; the ocean-house and palaces; the secret passages behind the walls; the paintings; the toy deer; the mechanical devices; the birds; and the cages of tigers, lions, and so forth, which have been described previously."
5.5.17. And in private, she should cause him to hear of her devotion to the Lord.
5.5.18. She should describe her skill in sexual union.
5.5.19. And once she has gained his consent, she should engage with him without speaking aloud.

5.5.20. If she does not comply, the king himself should come and, having won her over with courtesies and conciliation, he should unite with her and then dismiss her with affection. 5.5.21. Furthermore, he should regularly admit into the inner apartments, according to propriety, the wives of the man to be employed who is worthy of the king's favor; there, a female spy should be stationed.
The term "the king's female slave" is the same as the previous [case].
5.5.22. Alternatively, a woman of the inner apartments may cultivate affection with a courtesan by sending her own maidservant as a messenger.
Once the affection has developed, she should arrange for them to meet under some pretext.
When she has entered and been honored, and having drunk the *varti* (collyrium), she is introduced as "the King’s maidservant," the rest is the same as before.
Or, in whatever skill she is renowned for, the woman of the inner apartments should summon her with due ceremony for the purpose of demonstrating that skill;
when she has entered, she is introduced as "the King’s maidservant," the rest being the same as before. 5.5.23.

5.5.24. To a woman who has been separated from her husband or is afraid of him, a female mendicant should say: "That lady of the inner apartments is a confidante of the king; she accepts his word and listens to my speech.
By nature she is compassionate, and I shall win her over by this means.
I myself will arrange your entrance."
"She will avert a great calamity for your husband"—having been thus addressed, she should be admitted two or three times;
and a woman of the inner apartments should grant her assurance of safety. Upon hearing that assurance...
And she who is delighted and intent [on her task], thinking "I am the king's slave-girl"—the rest is the same as before.

(5.5.25) By this [method], the wives of those seeking livelihood, those oppressed by high officials, those seized by force, those weak in legal disputes, those dissatisfied with their own enjoyments, those desiring favor with the king, those wishing for [influence over] the people of the kingdom, those being harassed by kinsmen, those wishing to harass kinsmen, informers, and others who are masters of their own affairs, are explained. (p. 292)

5.5.26. Or, having secured a woman who has been associated with another man or who has been brought into servitude, he should gradually introduce her into the inner apartments. 5.5.27. By means of a spy, he should corrupt her future prospects and report that she is "displeasing" to the king; then, under the pretext of taking her away from the husband, he should cause her to enter the inner apartments. These are secret stratagems, generally employed in the case of princes.

5.5.28. However, a lord should never enter the house of another in such a manner. (p.294) 5.5.29. For instance, a washerman, acting on the instigation of his brother, killed the Ābhīra Koṭṭarāja while he was in another's house;
likewise, the superintendent of horses killed Jayasena, the King of Kāśi. (p.294)
5.5.30. However, those who desire public exposure [do so] through their connection with local customs.

5.5.31. Among the Āndhras, the maidens of the countryside, once given in marriage, enter the inner apartments on the tenth day after receiving some small gift as a token; having been enjoyed, they are then dismissed. 5.5.32. Among the Vātsagulmakas, the harem women approach the king at night for the purpose of service, seeking the favor of high-ranking officials and lords.
5.5.33. Among the Vaidarbhas, beautiful women of the countryside stay for a month or half a month within the inner apartments under the pretext of affection.
5.5.34. Among the Aparāntakas, handsome wives give themselves as gifts of affection to high officials and kings.
Among the Saurāṣṭrakas, city women and country women enter the royal palace both in groups and individually.
On this point there are two verses:
5.5.36ab. These and many other practices pertaining to adultery, 5.5.36cd. prevail in various regions, having been established by kings.
5.5.37ab. However, a king devoted to the welfare of the world should never employ these [harsh measures].
5.5.37cd. Having thus restrained the group of six internal enemies, he conquers the earth. 5.6. Concerning the harem and the protection of the wives.

5.6.1. Because of the necessity of guarding the women of the inner apartments, they have no opportunity for the sight of men; furthermore, because their husband is a single individual common to many, they remain unsatisfied.
Therefore, they should mutually gratify one another through the employment of various means.

5.6.2. Having dressed a nurse’s daughter, a female friend, or a maidservant like a man, they should satisfy their own desires by means of bulbs, roots, fruits, or parts thereof that resemble male organs, or by artificial phalli.
5.6.3. Men who wear unmanifested signs [of their profession] should lie down beside effigies of women.

5.6.4. Kings who are compassionate by nature may, even without the application of passion, employ artificial means and approach a woman for the sake of their purpose during one night or even many nights.
However, they proceed according to her desire regarding the specific night or season; such is the traditional practice of the Easterners.

5.6.5. By means of union with women alone, even for men whose livelihood has not been secured, the fulfillment of their desire is explained as occurring through intercourse with those of different species, different castes, or artificial female forms, by means of mere physical contact. (p. 297) 5.6.6. Generally, the women of the inner apartments cause these city-dwellers to enter along with their female attendants.
5.6.7. To win them over, the daughters of nurses who have intimate access to the interior should strive, pointing out the future prospects.

5.6.8. They should describe the ease of access to the grounds for retreat, the spaciousness of the residence, the negligence of the guards, and the instability of the attendants. 5.6.9. And they should not, by means of false matters, entice people to enter, because of the resulting fault.
5.6.10. Vātsyāyana, however, maintains that a man of noble birth should not enter the inner apartments, even if they are easily accessible, because of the abundance of dangers therein.

5.6.11 However, having observed the reasons— such as that the pleasure garden has an exit, its long corridors are partitioned, the guards are few and negligent, and the king is away— and having been summoned many times with the intent of gaining wealth, and seeing the opportunity for entry into the inner quarters, he should enter by means devised by those very women.
5.6.12. And when it is within his power, he should go out every day.
5.6.13. Outside, he should associate with guards under some other pretext.
5.6.14. When a female attendant who moves within the palace has become aware of his intentions, he should make her believe that he is attached to her.

Due to that failure to obtain [her], he should experience grief and perform all the duties of a female messenger (*dūtī*) by means of women who enter her inner quarters. (5.6.15) He should also discern the king’s intentions. (5.6.16) However, when no female messenger can be dispatched, he should remain in a place where he can meet with the woman to be approached, provided she has not yet revealed her intentions.
5.6.17. Even among those guards, however, she should employ the pretext of being an attendant. 5.6.18. While her gaze is fixed upon him, she should communicate his gestures and expressions.
5.6.19. Wherever he happens to be, there she should place paintings of him, musical pieces suited to him, and playthings marked with his name, as well as stuffed pillows.
And he should observe the reply given by her regarding the deposit of the ring;
thereafter, he should strive for entry. (p. 299)
5.6.21. Wherever one knows her destination is certain, there he should station himself beforehand in concealment. 5.6.22. Or, disguised as a guard, he may enter at a time permitted by her.
5.6.23. Or, his entry and exit may be accomplished while he is wrapped in a bedspread or a cloak.
5.6.24. Or, by means of the *puṭapāka* and *apuṭapāka* methods, one becomes invisible in form and shadow.
5.6.25. The procedure for this is as follows: one should cook the heart of a mongoose, the fruits of *corakatumbī*, and *sarpākṣī* over indirect heat (*antardhūma*).
Then, one should grind them with an equal portion of collyrium (*añjana*).
With his eyes anointed by this, he moves about with his complexion and form rendered invisible;
or [he may do so] by means of other external draughts such as *jala*, *brahma*, *kṣema*, or *śiraḥpraṇīta*;
or during moonlit nights in a place crowded with lamps, or by means of a subterranean tunnel.
In this regard, the following occurs:
5.6.27a. Even when goods are being carried out, when drinks are being brought in, 5.6.27b. even for the sake of a drinking festival, or during the bustle of female servants; (p.300)
5.6.27c. Also when there is a rearrangement of houses or a change in the guards;
5.6.27d. upon going on an excursion to a garden, or upon returning from such an excursion;
5.6.27e. during a long-duration expedition, or when the king has gone abroad.

5.6.27f. Generally, there should be entry and likewise exit for the youths. (p.300) 5.6.28a. Having learned of each other's affairs, those residing in the inner apartments (p.300) 5.6.28b. Should act with a single purpose and then effect the sowing of dissension even among the rest. (p.300)
5.6.28cd. Having first caused mutual suspicion, he remains firm in the execution of a single common purpose;
having attained an immediate state of being indivisible [from his allies], he enjoys the fruit as he desires.
5.6.29. In that regard, among the people of Aparāntaka, it is the women who frequent the royal court who introduce distinguished men into the inner apartments, because of their extreme security.

5.6.30. Among the Ābhīras, they accomplish their purpose with those known as Kṣatriyas who serve as guards of the inner apartments. 5.6.31. Among the Vātsagulmakas, they cause sons of city-dwellers, dressed in the garb of servants, to enter together with female attendants.
5.6.32. Among the Vaidarbhas, they enjoy the inner apartments according to their own will with their own sons, excluding only their mothers.
5.6.33. Likewise, among the Strīrājaka kings, [the women] are enjoyed only by kinsmen and relatives who have entered [the harem], and not by others.
5.6.34. Among the Gauḍas, they are enjoyed by Brāhmaṇas, friends, servants, slaves, and attendants.
5.6.35. Among the Saindhavas, the laborers and workmen are unrestricted within the harems, as are others of similar status.

5.6.36. Having bribed the guards with wealth, bands of robbers enter the territories of the people of the Himalayas in groups. 5.6.37. Under the pretext of delivering flowers, city Brahmins go to the harems known to the king;
their conversation with the women takes place through a curtain.
Through that connection, there is an intermingling of the Vaṅgas, Aṅgas, and Kaliṅgas;
by joining together nine or ten [women], they conceal each young man of the Easterners. (5.6.38) [p.301]
In this same manner, one should treat the wives of others.
Thus ends the section on the conduct regarding women of the harem (antaḥpurikā-vṛtta).
(p.302) 5.6.39. And for these very reasons, one should protect one's own wife. (p.302)
5.6.40. "The teachers maintain that one should appoint guards in the inner apartments who have been proven pure by the test of lust (*kāma-upadhā*).

5.6.41. "For they might, out of fear or for the sake of wealth, incite another [to commit misconduct]; therefore, they should be those proven pure by the tests of lust, fear, and wealth," says Goṇikāputra.
5.6.42. "Non-injury is the law (*dharma*); one might even abandon that law out of fear; therefore, they should be those proven pure by the tests of law and fear," says Vātsyāyana. (p. 303)

5.6.43. According to the followers of Bābhravya, one should employ women who conceal their true intentions and speak the words of others to keep watch over one's own wives, for the purpose of discerning their purity or impurity.
5.6.44. Vātsyāyana maintains that since wicked men have already gained access to young women, one should not groundlessly bring about the corruption of those who are innocent.
5.6.45. Excessive socializing, lack of restraint, the husband’s own wantonness, and being unrestrained in the company of other men [are causes of corruption].
Living abroad, residing in a foreign land, the impairment of one's own livelihood, association with wanton women, and the husband’s jealousy—these are the causes of ruin for women.
(5.6.46a) Having observed from the treatises the methods characterized by those who commit adultery, no one who knows the science would resort to deception regarding his own wife. (5.6.46b)

5.6.47 Because the results of actions are uncertain and because misfortunes are observed [to follow from them], and because it leads to the subversion of both dharma and artha, one should not commit adultery.
(p.304) 5.6.48 This [prohibition] has been undertaken for the sake of guarding one's wife and for the welfare of men. (p.304)
5.6.48b / His entire arrangement [of affairs] is not to be understood as being for the purpose of corrupting the subjects.
6. The Section on Courtesans (Vaiśika):
6.1. Consideration of companions, those who may be approached and those who may not; the reasons for approaching; and the winning over of one who is to be approached.

6.1.1. For courtesans, pleasure and livelihood arise simultaneously with the acquisition of a man. 6.1.2. Engagement for the sake of pleasure is natural; that which is for the sake of wealth is artificial.
6.1.3. Even that [artificial engagement] should be made to appear as if it were natural.

6.1.4 For men place their trust in women who are devoted to pleasure; therefore, he should demonstrate his lack of greed for that purpose. 6.1.5 And he should not accomplish his objectives by improper means, in order to preserve his future prospects.

6.1.7. She should always be adorned with ornaments and look out toward the royal highway; while being seen, she should not stand too exposed. 6.1.8. She should employ those companions by whom she may win over the hero, exclude him from others, counteract her own misfortunes, and accomplish her goals, and who will not treat her with contempt because of their accessibility. 6.1.9. These, however, are the guards, the officials of the court of justice, astrologers, the valiant, the brave, and those of equal learning.

Those who seize upon small portions [of wealth] include the *pīṭhamarda*, the *viṭa*, the *vidūṣaka*, the garland-maker, the perfumer, the vintner, the washerman, the barber, and the mendicant; these and others are included because of their utility for the task.

However, those who approach solely for the sake of wealth are as follows: one who is independent, in the prime of life, wealthy, living openly, holding a position of authority, and having acquired his wealth without difficulty.
He is competitive, persistent, conceited about his good fortune, boastful, and impotent yet desiring the reputation of being a man;
he is naturally envious and generous;
he is successful with kings or high ministers, and places his trust in fate.

One who treats his elders with contempt, one who transgresses their instructions, one who has become a target for his kinsmen, one who possesses wealth, an only son, one who bears the marks of an ascetic, one whose desires are concealed, a hero, and a physician—[these are the types of men].
(6.1.11) Pleasure, fame, and wealth, however, are to be attained through [cultivating] virtues. (6.1.11)

6.1.12. He should be of noble birth, learned, conversant with all conventions, a poet skilled in narrative, eloquent, bold, knowledgeable in various arts, experienced in the ways of the elderly, liberal, possessed of great energy, firm in devotion, free from envy, generous, affectionate toward friends, and inclined toward social gatherings, assemblies, spectacles, public festivals, and intellectual contests; he should be free from disease and have a body without physical defects.

A hero (nāyaka) who possesses vital breath, does not drink intoxicants, is virile, friendly toward women, a leader of women, and one who fondles them; yet he is not under their control, acts with independence, is not cruel, is free from envy, and is without suspicion— these are the qualities of a hero.

6.1.13. Furthermore, the qualities of a heroine (*nāyikā*) are as follows: she is devoted to virtues such as beauty, youth, auspicious marks, sweetness, and yoga; she does not possess such attachment to material objects; she is characterized by constancy and an abundance of excellence; she seeks distinction; she is always free from miserly conduct; and she delights in social gatherings and the arts. [These are the qualities of a heroine. (p. 309)

6.1.14. Furthermore, the qualities common to a heroine are: intelligence, character, and conduct; uprightness, gratitude, foresight regarding the long term and the distant; reliability; knowledge of place and time; urbanity; the avoidance of wretchedness, excessive laughter, calumny, slander, anger, greed, arrogance, and fickleness;
being the first to speak; skill in the *Kāmasūtra*; and proficiency in the arts pertaining to its constituent parts. These are the common qualities.

6.1.16. One who is consumptive, diseased, infested with worms, whose excrement is [eaten by] crows, who is fond of his wife, harsh in speech, miserly, pitiless, abandoned by his elders, a thief, deceitful in nature, addicted to root-magic (mūlakarman), indifferent to honor and dishonor, easily deprived of his wealth even by those he hates, and shameless— such persons are not to be approached.

6.1.17. "Passion, fear, wealth, rivalry, the settling of a grudge, the desire to know, factionalism, weariness, heat, fame, compassion, the words of a friend, shame, resemblance to a loved one, gratitude, the removal of passion, kinship, shared residence, continuity, and future prospects— these are the causes for going, according to the Teachers."
6.1.18 Vātsyāyana maintains that the purpose [of sexual union] consists of wealth, the warding off of misfortune, and pleasure.
6.1.19 However, wealth is not excluded by pleasure,
because it holds primary importance.

6.1.20. However, in situations involving fear and the like, one must examine the relative gravity or lightness of the circumstances; this concerns whether an ally is accessible or inaccessible for sexual union.
6.1.21. Even when solicited by an accessible man, she should not consent immediately, because men are prone to easily becoming contemptuous.
6.1.22. To ascertain the state of mind [of the woman], he should employ through the agency of messengers couriers, masseurs, singers, jesters, or those devoted to her, within the reach of the hero;
or, in their absence, pīṭhamardas and others.
From them, he should learn the hero's purity or impurity, his passion or lack thereof, whether she is attached or unattached, and whether she gives gifts or not.
6.1.24. He should cultivate a friendship with one who is highly esteemed, preceded by the activities of a *viṭa* (libertine).

6.1.25. Under the pretext of watching cockfights, quail-fights, ram-fights, or the singing of parrots and mynas, or on account of some artistic performance, the *pīṭhamarda* (the companion-in-arms) should bring the hero to her residence, or her to his. 6.1.26. Or he may bring her to him.
6.1.27. When he has arrived, she should personally give him a gift of affection—a collection of objects that produces joy and curiosity—saying, "This is for your exclusive enjoyment.
6.1.28. She should delight him with those social gatherings in which he takes pleasure, and with various marks of courtesy.
6.1.29. Once he has departed, she should frequently send a female attendant to him, accompanied by a gift, engaging in playful conversation and jesting.
6.1.30. Approaching a man who is available for sexual union consists of going to him in person under the pretext of being accompanied by a *pīṭhamarda*.
And there are verses on this subject:
6.1.31ab. Betel leaves, flower garlands, and refined ointments— 6.1.31cd. One should bring these with affection to a guest who has arrived, and one should engage them in artistic conversations.

6.1.32ab. She should give away articles during a friendly visit and should effect an exchange; (p.314) 6.1.32cd. And she should employ her own [ornaments] for the purpose of the union, as if they were not hers; (p.314) 6.1.33ab. [She should do so] solely through gifts of affection, pretexts, and acts of service. (p.314)
6.1.33cd. Having become intimate with him who is to be approached, she should thereafter please him.
6.2. Conduct Toward the Lover.
6.2.1. United with the hero, she should observe the conduct of one who moves alone for the sake of pleasing him.
6.2.2. "She should please him but not become attached; she should act as if she were attached"—this is the summary statement.
6.2.3. She should remain dependent upon a mother who is of cruel character and devoted to wealth. 6.2.4. In her absence, she should depend on her grandmother.
6.2.5. But she should not take excessive pleasure with one who is approachable. 6.2.6. And he should bring his daughter there by force.
6.2.7. In that situation, however, the heroine will experience constant dissatisfaction, despondency, shame, and fear.

6.2.8. But one must never transgress the command. 6.2.9. One should declare that a certain disease is causeless, not loathsome, imperceptible to the eye, and transient. 6.2.10. When there is a valid reason, one may approach the leaders under that pretext.

6.2.11. But the mistress should send her maidservant with the remains of the garland (*nirmālya*) and the betel. 6.2.12. She should show astonishment during sexual intercourse and its attendant services.
6.2.13. Regarding the sixty-four arts (*catuḥṣaṣṭi*), she should maintain the status of a pupil.
6.2.14. The constant practice of those methods (yoga) taught by him; 6.2.15. Conducting oneself in seclusion due to being habituated to that [practice];
6.2.16. The recounting of one's desires.
6.2.17. Concealing deformities of the private parts. 6.2.18. Not neglecting a man who has turned away during sexual intercourse. 6.2.19. Compliance when there is touching of the private parts.

6.2.20. Kissing and embracing [her] while she is asleep. 6.2.21. Gazing at her when she is distracted; and for one standing on a palace terrace, gazing at her as she is recognized there on the royal highway, which results in the destruction of her shame and deceit.
6.2.22. There is aversion toward that which is hated by him;
there is affection toward that which is dear to him; and there is delight in that which is pleasing to him.
Following that, there is joy and sorrow;
an inquiry into women;
and anger that is not long-lasting.
6.2.23. Even regarding nail and tooth marks made by oneself, one should feign suspicion of another.
6.2.25. However, one should display [the marks] through outward appearance.
6.2.26. But in cases of intoxication, sleep, or illness, there is no need for such an explanation.
6.2.27. [The same applies] to praiseworthy deeds performed by the leader.
6.2.28. While he is speaking, there is the grasping of the meaning of his words; having understood that, one speaks in praise regarding the subject at hand.
And the application of that statement is with the following [verse]:
"If she is devoted, there is compliance with her words in conversations, except regarding a co-wife. (6.2.29)

6.2.30. If [the messenger] sighs, yawns, stumbles, or falls, one should expect misfortune for him. 6.2.31. Upon sneezing, speaking out of turn, or being startled, one should utter the word "Live! (jīva). 6.2.32. In the case of dejection, one should offer the pretext of illness or pregnancy-longing.
6.2.33. Not proclaiming the virtues of another.
6.2.34. Not censuring one who possesses the same faults as oneself.
6.2.35. Maintaining what has been given.
6.2.36. For a frivolous offense or for addiction to that vice, there shall be confiscation of her ornaments and denial of food.
6.2.37. She shall also be subjected to reproachful lamentations concerning those matters.
6.2.38. She may, however, seek the king’s permission to leave the country along with him and obtain a ransom for her release.

6.2.39. The capacity for attaining long life lies in its acquisition. 6.2.40. Upon the attainment of one's purpose, the accomplishment of a desired goal, or the restoration of the body, there shall be an offering to the chosen deity as previously agreed upon. 6.2.41. There shall be constant application of ornaments.
Food should be moderate.
When singing, one should mention both the name and the lineage.
In the event of exhaustion, one should place the hand upon the chest and the forehead.
Having obtained that pleasure, one attains sleep;
moreover, there is sitting upon his lap and sleeping [there],
and going away when separated from him.
6.2.44. Therefore, one who desires a son should not wish for an excess of longevity.
6.2.45. One should not speak of this unknown matter in secret.
6.2.46. She should cause him to fulfill his vow and fast, thinking, "The fault lies with me.
If she is unable to do so, she herself should assume that same form [of fasting].
6.2.47. In the event of a dispute, the meaning is that even by him [the husband] it cannot be accomplished.
6.2.48. He should personally regard her as his own, without making any distinction.
6.2.49. Without her, he should not attend social gatherings and the like.
6.2.50. He should take pride in wearing her discarded flower-garlands and eating the remnants of her food.
6.2.52. Honoring [the messenger] according to his friendship, qualities, age, and pleasantness.
6.2.53. Urging one who is knowledgeable regarding singing and other arts [to perform].
[6.2.54. Approaching him regardless of fear, cold, heat, or rain.
6.2.54. "May he alone be mine" is the declaration she makes regarding funeral rites for the deceased.
6.2.57. And in approaching him, there is constant quarreling with her mother.
6.2.58. If she should be led elsewhere by force, then she would desire poison, fasting, a weapon, or a rope.

6.2.59. And there shall be the winning over of the leader by means of secret agents, or else he himself shall assume the role of a servant. 6.2.60. But there must never be a dispute regarding the objectives.
6.2.61. Without her mother’s permission, she should not engage in any activity whatsoever.

6.2.62. When he is away on a journey, she should utter a curse so that he may return quickly. 6.2.63. While he is absent, she should observe rules regarding cleanliness and refrain from wearing ornaments.
One should observe auspiciousness;
one may wear a single conch-shell bangle.
[6.2.64] One should recollect those who have passed away.
The departure of female fortune-tellers and astrologers;
the longing for the constellations, the moon, the sun, and the stars;
and the utterance of words such as, "May I have union with him upon seeing a desired dream. (6.2.65)
6.2.66. There shall be agitation regarding what is undesirable, as well as rites for pacification.
6.2.67. Upon his return, there shall be worship according to one's desire.
6.2.68. There shall be the offering of oblations to the deities.
6.2.69. The bringing of the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*) by her female friends.
6.2.70. And the worship of the crows (*vāyasapūjā*).
6.2.71. And after the first union, this same [ceremony] takes place, with the exception of the worship of the crows.
6.2.72. And one should speak of the "following in death" (anumāraṇa) by one who is attached.

6.2.73. One whose affection has been bestowed, who shares the same conduct, who acts for the sake of the purpose, who is free from apprehension, and who is indifferent toward material gains—these are the characteristics of the "attached" (sakta).
6.2.74. This has been stated in the *Dattaka-śāsana* for the purpose of illustration.
And one should practice that which is not explicitly stated according to worldly custom and according to human nature.
And you have two verses on this point:

6.2.75ab. Because of their subtlety, because of excessive greed, and likewise because of innate ignorance, 6.2.75cd. the mark of desire among women is difficult to discern, even by those who are accustomed to it.

6.2.76ab. They desire, they become dispassionate, they cause passion, and they abandon; (p.323) 6.2.76cd. Even while drawing away all objects of interest, women are never truly known. (p.323) 6.3. The means for acquiring wealth, the signs of dispassion, the conduct of one who is dispassionate, and the sequence of expulsion.
6.3.1. The acquisition of wealth from those who are attached [to him] and others occurs both naturally and through strategic means.
6.3.2. Regarding this, the teachers maintain that one who receives more than what was intended, or even more than expected, should not employ strategic means.
6.3.3. Vātsyāyana, however, holds that even if it is known, one should employ means, for [the donor], being thus refined by such methods, will give double [the amount]. (p. 324)

6.3.4. Among those engaged in trade, there shall be a temporary loan for the purpose of recovering capital in exchange for ornaments, food, edibles, drinks, garlands, clothing, perfumes, and other such articles. 6.3.5. In their presence, there shall be praise of that wealth.
6.3.7. On account of visiting them, there may be the theft of ornaments by guards or thieves.
6.3.8. Through arson, breaking down walls, or negligence, there shall be the destruction of property in the house.
6.3.9. Likewise, through spies, he shall report on the ornaments requested [for her], the ornaments of the hero (nāyaka), and the expenditure incurred for the purpose of visiting him.
6.3.10. For that purpose, she shall incur debts.
There will be a dispute with his mother regarding the expenses arising from that [marriage] (6.3.11).
He will not attend to the affairs of his friends because he lacks the means for providing them (6.3.12).
Furthermore, the teachers and the gifts previously brought by those [friends]—(p.324) [he will neglect them].

Those who have been previously initiated should be instructed [in their duties]. (6.3.13) There should be no interruption of customary practices. (6.3.14) And work should be carried out among artisans for the sake of the leader.
6.3.15. One should perform services for the physician and the high minister for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose.
6.3.16. One should provide assistance to friends and benefactors in times of misfortune.

6.3.17. Domestic duties include: assisting a friend’s wife during pregnancy, attending to the delivery of a son, alleviating the longings of pregnancy, caring for a friend’s illness, and removing a friend’s suffering.
6.3.18. Selling a portion of an ornament for the sake of the *nāyaka*.

6.3.19. Showing an ornament or household utensil that she has used to a merchant for the purpose of sale. 6.3.20. Upon the exchange of similar goods with rival courtesans, taking those of superior quality.

6.3.21. One should not forget previous favors and should recount them. 6.3.22. Through intermediaries, one should cause the other courtesans to hear of the superior gains [one has received]. 6.3.23. In their presence, before the hero, one should describe one's own excessive gains—whether real or imagined—under the name "the bashful one."
6.3.24. There is no explicit prohibition against those former practitioners who, through an excellence in their acquisitions, strive once again to re-establish contact.
6.3.25. An illustration of this is the case of those who, competing with them, employ the yoga of renunciation.
6.3.26. "It will not come back"—this refers to the "borrowing of a child"; such are the means for the acquisition of wealth. (p. 325)
6.3.27. One should know that he is constantly detached from the transformations of nature (prakṛti-vikriyā) by his facial expression and complexion.
6.3.28. He gives either less or more [than what is due].
6.3.29. He associates with those of lower castes (pratiloma).
6.3.30. He does something else after having promised one thing. 6.3.31. He cuts off what is appropriate. 6.3.32. He forgets what has been promised.
Or he interprets things otherwise;
(6.3.33) he speaks using the terminology of his own side; (6.3.34) and under the pretext of attending to a friend's business, he lies elsewhere.
6.3.35. And she converses privately with her attendants who were previously acquainted with her.
6.3.36. Before he becomes aware of it, she should take his valuable goods into her own hands under some pretext.
6.3.37. Then, as a creditor, she should forcibly seize those items from his hand.
6.3.38. "One should conduct legal proceedings with a litigant in the presence of judges"—this is the course of action for one who is detached.
6.3.39. But one who is attached should maintain even a former benefactor, even if he yields little fruit, by means of conciliation.
6.3.40. However, one who is worthless and offers no response should be removed by employing strategic means.
Supporting another [limb] (p.329):
the practice of censuring;
the movement of the lips.
Striking the ground with the foot;
engaging in conversation about a subject one does not understand;
and showing neither wonder nor contempt toward things that have been understood.
The destruction of pride;
dwelling together with those who are superior;
and lack of regard.
Censuring those who share the same faults; dwelling in secret;
and taking hold of the face.
The protection of the hips;
a loathing for wounds caused by nails or teeth;
and, during an embrace, the interposition of the arm as a needle.
Stiffness of the limbs, crossing of the thighs,
and an inability to sleep.
Upon perceiving fatigue, there is exhortation;
upon incapacity, laughter; and upon capacity, a lack of enthusiasm.
Even during the day, having perceived the presence [of people], there is the arrival of a great multitude; (p.331) 6.3.43. /In sentences, there is the grasping of a quibble (chala).
Laughter at an inappropriate time;
and during a jest, laughing while pointing to someone else, or looking askance at her attendants while speaking to him;
and after mentioning his story, shifting to other topics.
The recounting of those insults and unavoidable calamities;
the mention of her vital vulnerabilities by the maidservant;
and her disappearance upon his arrival. 6.3.44.
"Entreaty from one who should not be entreated," and "liberation by oneself at the end"— these refer to the adopted son (dattaka) as the recipient of the inheritance.
And on this subject, you have two verses:
6.3.45ab / Having examined [the man], there is union with those who are approachable; for one who is united, there is pleasing him.
6.3.45cd / From one who is impassioned, there is the acquisition of wealth, and finally, release—this is the practice of the courtesan (*vaiśika*).
6.3.46ab. Thus, by following this method, a courtesan established in her profession is not outwitted by those who seek her company, and she generates abundant wealth.
6.4. Reconciliation after a breach.
6.4.1. Abandoning her current lover whose purpose has been fulfilled, she should form an alliance with one previously acquainted.
(p.333) 6.4.2. If he has completed his business, is wealthy, and is full of passion, then she should unite with him.
(p.333) 6.4.3. If he has gone elsewhere, she should consider [the situation].
That [withdrawal] is of six kinds according to its application to the task:
(6.4.4) withdrawal from here by oneself and from there also by oneself; (6.4.5) and withdrawal after being expelled from here and from there.
6.4.6. Having departed from here of one's own accord, one is then expelled from there. 6.4.7. Having departed from here of one's own accord, one remains stationed there.
6.4.8. Having been expelled from here and departed, one then departs of one's own accord from there.

6.4.9. One who has been expelled from here and has departed, yet remains stationed there; (p.334) 6.4.10. If, having himself departed from here and there, he makes overtures while considering the merits of both sides, he is of fickle mind and should not be allied with.
(p.334) 6.4.11. One who has been expelled from here and there and has departed is of steady mind.

If he has been dismissed by her because she was receiving much from another source, even though he is wealthy, he should be reconciled with her, thinking: "He will be provoked by her and, out of resentment toward me, will give much.
(6.4.12) One who has been abandoned due to lack of resources or miserliness is not beneficial.
(6.4.13) If one has departed of his own accord from here and has been dismissed from there, and if he should give more than usual and offer it first, then he should be accepted.
6.4.14. Having withdrawn from here himself and remaining there, he should be observed while whispering [to others].

6.4.15. If one who has come seeking something special, having failed to see that special thing there, desires to come back to me—desiring to test me—he will, upon arriving, give [more] because of his affection;
or, having seen faults in her and now seeing many virtues in me, being a perceiver of virtues, he will give most abundantly.

6.4.16. Having ascertained whether he is a fool, or one whose gaze is not fixed on a single object, or one primarily intent on deception, or one whose passion is fleeting like turmeric, or one who acts recklessly, one should either form an alliance with him or not.

6.4.17. One who has been expelled from here and gone elsewhere, and having departed from there of his own accord, should be scrutinized when he attempts to instigate a rebellion. 6.4.18. If, out of affection, he desires to come back, he will give much.
"One who has been imbued with my virtues does not take pleasure in another.
(p.336) 6.4.19. Either he was previously dismissed by me without cause, and having cultivated his character, now wishes to avenge the enmity;
or wealth was taken from him by me through a legal suit, and wishing to win his trust in order to take it back or to recover it, he acts thus."
Or, if he intends to expose me while I am present and then abandon me, he is one of evil intent and should not be allied with.
(6.4.20) / One whose mind is otherwise should be won over by means of time.
(6.4.21) / One who has been expelled from here and, staying there, instigates [trouble] is explained by this same rule. (6.4.21)

6.4.22. While they are attempting to instigate [the enemy], he himself, remaining elsewhere, should instigate them as well. 6.4.23. "He was dismissed by me for the sake of some offense; wherever he has gone, he must be brought back with effort.
6.4.24. "Or, having begun a conversation from here, he will suffer a rift [with his current associates] because of that."
6.4.25. If he will cause the obstruction of the purpose of one who is currently engaged [in an action], or if this is the time for the attainment of his purpose;
6.4.26. Or if it is the time for the acquisition of wealth for him.
His status has increased;
he has obtained an official position;
he is separated from his wife.
He is free from dependence on others; he has been separated from his father or brother. (6.4.27) Or else: "By means of this man, or by forming an alliance with him, I shall obtain a wealthy patron."
6.4.28. "If he has been insulted by his wife, I shall cause him to exert his prowess against her.

6.4.29. "Or, if he desires a co-wife who hates me, I shall cause him to be alienated from her by means of that [co-wife]. 6.4.30. "Or, because of his fickle nature, I shall bring about his disgrace. (p. 338)

6.4.31. His confidants, such as the *pīṭhamarda* and others, should describe how, due to the mother’s immoral conduct, the heroine was previously driven out despite her affection for him and her being rendered helpless.
6.4.32. And they should describe her current association with him against her will and her resulting resentment.
6.4.33. And they should cause her to be reconciled with him by means of tokens of recognition and former expressions of affection.

6.4.34. The token of recognition should be connected with a service rendered by him; thus there is a rejoining of what has been severed. 6.4.35. Between one who has never met before and one who has previously associated, the one with whom she had a prior association is superior.
"For he whose character is known and whose passion has been observed becomes easy to deal with," so say the teachers (ācāryāḥ).

Vātsyāyana, however, maintains that one who has been previously acquainted is difficult to win over again because his wealth has been squeezed out from all sides, and it is painful to inspire confidence in him; whereas a man who has not been previously acquainted is easily won over with affection.
6.4.37. Nevertheless, there is a distinction based on the nature of the individual.
And there are verses on this point:

"To cause a division between [the ally] and another, or to divert the one to be approached toward someone else; and for the purpose of striking down one who is established [in his position], a treaty is again desired."
6.4.39ab. He fears the company of others and does not observe their offenses;

(p.340) 6.4.39cd. A man who is excessively attached to someone gives much out of fear. (p.340) 6.4.40ab. One should rejoice in one who is unattached, and likewise treat with contempt one who is attached. (p.340)
6.4.40cd. And when another messenger arrives, she should employ one who is exceedingly skillful.
(p.340) 6.4.41ab. She should unite with the man who first approached her at the proper time;
(p.340) 6.4.41cd. She should maintain an unbroken connection and never abandon one who is devoted to her. (A pair of verses) (p.340)

6.4.42ab. But a woman, having conversed with a man who is attached yet self-controlled, may depart for elsewhere. (p.340) 6.4.42cd. Then, having secured some benefit from him, she should win over that very man to whom she was attached.
(p.340) 6.4.43ab. Having first carefully considered the future, as well as the abundant gain and pleasure [to be derived]. (p.340)
6.4.43cd. A discerning woman should repair a friendship that has been shattered.
6.5. Special Gains:
6.5.1. When there is an abundance of available men, she who receives much gain every day should not accept [the advances of] only one.
6.5.2. Having considered the place, the time, his own status, his qualities, his good fortune, and whether he is inferior or superior to other women, he should establish his purpose during the night.
6.5.3. He should employ messengers toward the woman with whom he intends to go, and he himself should send those who are already connected to her.
6.5.4. To ensure the acquisition of an exceptional gain, she may go to even a single man two, three, or four times, and she should also exercise her choice [of whom to favor].

6.5.5. But when there is simultaneous access to multiple men and the gains are equal, the teachers maintain that the distinction lies in the recipient who possesses the specific object desired by her.
6.5.6 Vātsyāyana maintains that because all undertakings are non-returnable and because they are rooted therein, [the giver] is called a "bestower of gold" (*hiraṇyada*).

6.5.7 Among the various types of gold, silver, copper, bronze, iron vessels, utensils, rugs, coverlets, specific kinds of clothing, fragrant substances, pungent condiments, ghee, oil, grains, and livestock,
each preceding category is superior to the one following it.

6.5.8. In that case, when there is parity [of other factors], the distinction [between two suitors] arises from the nature of the object, from parity of wealth, from the words of a friend, from being free from transgression, from lineage, from personal qualities, and from affection.
6.5.9. Regarding the passionate man and the renunciant, the teachers maintain that the distinction clearly lies with the renunciant;
for it is possible to instill renunciation in one who is passionate. (pp. 343–344)

6.5.11. Vātsyāyana maintains that even a greedy man who is impassioned will abandon [his passion], but a generous man does not; rather, it is the generous man who becomes impassioned through persistence. 6.5.12. Even in that regard, there is a distinction between one who possesses wealth and one who does not; the preference is for the wealthy man.
Furthermore, between a generous man and one who accomplishes a specific purpose, the teachers hold that the preference is clearly for the one who accomplishes the purpose.

6.5.13. Vātsyāyana maintains that the one who acts for a specific purpose, having performed his duty once, considers himself successful; the renouncer (*tyāgī*), however, does not look back upon what has passed. 6.5.14. Even in this regard, there is a distinction based on urgency. 6.5.15. The teachers hold that the distinction between the grateful person and the renouncer is evident in the case of the renouncer. (p.344)
6.5.16. Even if he has been served for a long time, a generous man, upon encountering a single offense or being falsely defamed by a rival courtesan, disregards all past labor.
6.5.17. For generally, those who are spirited, upright, and generous become indifferent when they are treated with disrespect.
6.5.18. But one who is grateful, mindful of former efforts, does not become disaffected all at once.
Vātsyāyana maintains that because his character has been thoroughly examined, he cannot be falsely accused.
(6.5.19) Even in that regard, there is a distinction based on the long-term consequences.
(6.5.20) Regarding the choice between the word of a friend and the acquisition of wealth, the teachers hold that the acquisition of wealth is a more evident benefit. (6.5.20)
6.5.21. "For even he will obtain wealth; however, Vātsyāyana maintains that once his speech has been rebuffed, a friend becomes defiled.
(p. 345) 6.5.22. "In that case as well, there is a distinction based on the degree of transgression. (p. 346)
6.5.23. Having conciliated the ally there by pointing out the task at hand, one should say, "Let it be tomorrow," and then accept the matter that must be accomplished with urgency.
6.5.24. Regarding the acquisition of wealth and the warding off of misfortune, the teachers maintain that the superiority in the acquisition of wealth is directly perceptible.
6.5.25. Wealth consists of a limited portion [of gain].
Vātsyāyana maintains that once a misfortune has spread, it is no longer known where it will come to rest.
Even in that case, however, there is a distinction based on the relative gravity or lightness of the situation.
By this, the distinction regarding the counteracting of misfortunes arising from doubt about one's interests is explained.
6.5.28. The construction of temples, tanks, and groves; the establishment of sacred sites and fire-altars;
and the gift of thousands of cows to Brahmins through an intermediary vessel.

The initiation of offerings and sacrifices for the deities, or the acquisition of wealth sufficient to sustain such expenditures—this is the excellence of profit for the highest class of courtesans. (p.347) 6.5.29. The application of ornaments to all parts of the body and the construction of a magnificent residence.
The excellence of gain for those who live by their beauty (*rūpājīvā*) consists of costly vessels, attendants, and the splendor of household furnishings (6.5.30).

For female slaves (*kumbhadāsī*), there is constant white clothing, food and drink free from hunger, constant use of fragrant scents and betel, and ornaments along with a share of gold (6.5.31). According to the teachers, one should apply these same categories of excellent gains to all women, including those of middle and lower status, according to their respective positions. (pp. 347–348)
6.5.32 Vātsyāyana maintains that the practice of restricting gains and so forth is not fixed, as it depends upon place, time, wealth, capability, affection, and the prevailing customs of the world.

6.5.33 A woman who desires to prevent another man from approaching her lover, or wishes to divert him from another woman, or seeks to separate him from someone else she has gained, may— considering her own security, prosperity, future prospects, and accessibility— engage in relations with one who is otherwise forbidden.

If she desires to make him an assistant in warding off misfortune; or if, seeking to cause harm to another to whom he is attached, she views his prior kindness as if it were never done; or if she seeks only her own pleasure; or if she, desiring future gain from one of virtuous intent, seeks to counteract a misfortune by relying on him—she should not accept [his advances] at all. (6.5.34) (p. 349)
6.5.35. "I shall abandon him and take up another; he will go away, or be joined with a wife, or perish in misfortunes;
or a superior supervisor, acting as a goad, will come for him, or his master or father."
Thinking, "He will suffer a fall from his position, or his mind will become unsteady," one should seek gain from him at that time [thinking]:
"He will receive the promised gift from the lord; he will obtain an office or a position;
the time for his salary is near; a vehicle will come to him; or his land, documents, or crops [will be secured]."
One should desire for the future that what has been done in this regard will not perish and will always be non-contradictory;
or else, one should act in accordance with the rules for formal acceptance.
And there are verses on this point:

One should avoid from afar those who have acquired their wealth through hardship, those who are cruel toward the king's favorites, and those who are intent on immediate gain both for the future and the present.

6.5.38ab. Those for whom there is no loss in avoiding [others] and likewise great prosperity in approaching them—(p.351) 6.5.38cd. Even with great effort, one should win them over by using some pretext and begin [the mission].
(p.351) 6.5.39ab. Those who, being well-disposed, bestow vast wealth even when asked for a very small amount—(p.351)
6.5.39cd. One should approach those who are liberal in their gifts and possessed of great energy, even by means of one's own expenditures.
6.6. Considerations regarding the consequences of gain and loss, as well as the specific types of courtesans.
6.6.1. When gains are being pursued, losses and uncertainties arise as their consequences (*anubandha*). (p. 352)

6.6.2. These [misfortunes] may arise from weakness of intellect, excessive passion, excessive pride, excessive deceit, excessive simplicity, excessive trust, excessive anger, negligence, recklessness, or the influence of fate.

6.6.3. The fruit of these [actions] consists of the fruitlessness of expenditure already incurred, the failure to obtain expected profit, the departure of one who has been acquired, the encounter with harshness, the destruction of the body, the cutting off of hair, its falling out, or the occurrence of physical deformity.
6.6.4. Therefore, one should seek to avoid them from the very beginning, and one should remain indifferent toward those things that abound in material gain (*artha*).

6.6.5. Material gain (*artha*), virtue (*dharma*), and pleasure (*kāma*) constitute the triad of the beneficial (*artha-trivarga*). 6.6.6. Loss (*anartha*), vice (*adharma*), and hatred (*dveṣa*) constitute the triad of the harmful (*anartha-trivarga*).
6.6.7. When those [means] are being employed, the accomplishment of something else as well is an "accessory" (*anubandha*).

6.6.8. When the attainment of the result is doubtful, such that one wonders "will it happen or not?", it is a "pure doubt" (*śuddha-saṃśaya*). 6.6.9. When it is thought "it might be this, or it might be that," it is a "mixed doubt" (*saṃkīrṇa*).
6.6.10. When one task is being performed and two tasks arise [simultaneously], that is "conjunction from both sides" (*ubhayato-yoga*).

6.6.11. Arising on all sides is "conjunction on all sides" (*samantato-yoga*); we shall provide examples of these. 6.6.12. The three aims of life (*trivarga*) have been examined in their essential form.

The opposite of that is the triad of non-beneficial [objects]. (p.354) 6.6.13. When, by approaching a superior person, there is a visible acquisition of wealth, as well as being accepted, future prospects, the arrival of further gains, and becoming an object of desire for others—that is beneficial wealth accompanied by further consequences (*arthānubandha*). (p.354) 6.6.14. Approaching someone else merely for the sake of gain—that is beneficial wealth without further consequences (*niranubandha*).

6.6.15. When one is attached to the acquisition of wealth for purposes other than [those of the state], it results in the cutting off of future prospects, the loss of revenue, or the departure of one who is hated by the world or of a base person—such wealth destroys the future and is followed by misfortune.

6.6.16. The departure of a brave man, a high official, or a powerful person at their own expense—even if fruitless—is for the sake of remedying a calamity; and the pacification of a great cause that destroys wealth generates future prosperity.
Or that misfortune may be followed by a benefit. (p.355) 6.6.17:

For one who is miserly yet considers himself fortunate, or for one who is ungrateful and habitually deceitful, even if he is propitiated with one's own expenditures, such service is ultimately fruitless; that is a misfortune without further consequence.

(p.355) 6.6.18: For that same royal favorite, if he is excessively cruel and powerful, propitiating him in that same manner is ultimately fruitless and leads to his dismissal, which causes harm; that is a misfortune followed by further misfortune.
6.6.19. In this same manner, one should also apply the consequential links (*anubandha*) to both *dharma* and *kāma*.

6.6.20. And one should combine them with one another through logical reasoning; these are the consequential links (*anubandha*). 6.6.21. Even when fully satisfied, [the donor] may or may not give; this is the uncertainty regarding wealth (*artha-saṃśaya*).

6.6.22. When one has squeezed out the purpose and abandoned it fruitlessly, or when one fails to obtain the desired object, there arises a doubt regarding righteousness (*dharma*): "Is this righteous or not? 6.6.23. Having obtained what was intended, or having gone to another servant or a lowly person [for pleasure], there arises a doubt regarding passion (*kāma*): "Is this passionate or not? 6.6.24. There arises a doubt regarding misfortune (*anartha*): "Will a powerful, lowly, and undesirable person cause me harm or not?"

6.6.25. One who is attached but utterly fruitless, having been abandoned, might go to the world of the ancestors; there would be a doubt regarding unrighteousness as to whether unrighteousness would occur there or not. 6.6.26. Even when there is a desire to speak out of passion, if one does not obtain what is intended, there may be dispassion or not; this is a doubt regarding aversion.
Thus are the doubts regarding purity. (p.

356) 6.6.28. When a newcomer whose character is unknown, who is a favorite, who has taken refuge [with us], or who is a powerful person presents himself, there arises the doubt as to whether his propitiation is a benefit or a disadvantage.

6.6.29. For a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), a student (*brahmacārin*), one initiated for a sacrifice (*dīkṣita*), one under a vow (*vratī*), or one bearing a religious mark (*liṅgin*), if they have conceived passion upon seeing me, there arises the doubt as to whether going to them—due to the word of a friend or out of compassion—is righteous (*dharma*) or unrighteous (*adharma*).
Thus there is doubt.

6.6.30. Doubt arises as to whether one’s departure from the world—without regard for whether it is free from qualities or possessed of qualities—is due to desire or aversion, based on a conviction formed merely from worldly experience.
6.6.31. And because they may be intermingled with one another, these are "intermingled doubts. (p. 357)
6.6.32. Where there is profit from approaching another and also from a rival suitor through competition, that is "profit on both sides" (ubhayato 'rthaḥ).

6.6.33. Where approaching with one's own expenditure is fruitless, yet a rival suitor, out of resentment, returns the wealth [previously given], that is "loss on both sides" (ubhayato 'narthaḥ). 6.6.34. Where there is doubt as to whether there will be profit from approaching or not, and even regarding a rival suitor, doubt as to whether he will give [wealth] due to competition or not, that is "doubt regarding profit on both sides" (ubhayato 'rthasaṃśayaḥ).

6.6.35. "In a case where visiting involves expense, one must consider whether the former [rival], being hostile, will cause harm out of anger, or not; or whether the latter, being attached yet resentful, will recover what was given, or not.
This is the "double-sided" [strategy] according to Auḍālaki; these are the double-sided applications. 6.6.36. But the followers of Bābhravya say:
6.6.37. Where there is gain from approaching her, and also gain from not approaching her because of a creditor, that is "gain on both sides.
6.6.38. Where there is fruitless expenditure from approaching her, and an unavoidable loss from not approaching her, that is "loss on both sides.

6.6.39. Where there is no expenditure from approaching her, but there is uncertainty as to whether she will give or not; and where there is a creditor from not approaching her, but there is uncertainty as to whether he will give or not, that is "uncertainty regarding gain on both sides."
6.6.40. When an expedition involves great expense, there arises the doubt as to whether one will encounter a powerful enemy who is hostile and superior, or not;
and the doubt as to whether, by not going, he will cause harm out of anger or not—this is a "doubt regarding harm from both sides" (*ubhayato 'nartha-saṃśaya*).
6.6.41. In the combination of these very factors, there is gain from one side and harm from the other.

"From one [source] there is gain, from another there is doubt regarding gain; from one there is gain, from another there is doubt regarding loss"—these are the six mixed combinations (ṣaṭsaṃkīrṇayoga).

(p.360) 6.6.42. Having deliberated with his companions regarding these, he should proceed from whichever course yields the greatest gain, involves the least doubt regarding gain, or results in the mitigation of a great loss. (p.360)
6.6.43. In this same manner, one should also cite examples regarding virtue (*dharma*) and pleasure (*kāma*) using this very logic;

by intermingling and intertwining them with one another, there are combinations on both sides. 6.6.44. When libertines (*viṭas*) join together and take possession of a single woman, that is "possession by a circle" (*goṣṭhī-parigraha*).
6.6.45. As she moves here and there among them, she shall bring about the desired end through her individual rivalry with each.

6.6.46. During the auspicious spring season and other such times, she should cause her mother to say to them: "My daughter will go today to him who provides for me this and that. 6.6.47. And she should observe the actions resulting from their pursuit of her out of that rivalry.

6.6.48. "Benefit on one side, benefit on all sides; harm on one side, harm on all sides; benefit on half [the side], benefit on all sides; harm on half [the side], harm on all sides"—these are the applications (yogas) regarding every direction.
6.6.49. One should apply the doubt regarding benefit and the doubt regarding harm as previously described.
And likewise, those who desire the Dharma may also be confused.
Thus, for the sake of the consequences—whether they be beneficial or harmful—the following are the specific types of courtesans (*veśyā*):

the water-jar slave-girl (*kumbhadāsī*), the attendant (*paricārikā*), the unchaste woman (*kulatā*), the wanton woman (*svairiṇī*), the actress (*naṭī*), the artisan (*śilpakārikā*), the one ruined in public (*prakāśavinaṣṭā*), the woman living by her beauty (*rūpājīvā*), and the courtesan (*gaṇikā*). (p. 363)

6.6.51. Suitable companions for all women, the means of winning them over, the acquisition of wealth, methods of expulsion, reconciliation, the consequences of specific gains, and the deliberation upon the consequences, benefits, and doubts regarding profit and loss—this constitutes the section on courtesans (*vaiśika*).
And you have two verses on this point:
"Since men have pleasure as their purpose, and women likewise have pleasure as their purpose,
because the meaning of the treatise is its primary concern, union with women is what is intended here."

6.6.53ab. There are women devoted to passion, and there are also those devoted to wealth. (p.364) 6.6.53cd. In that regard, passion has been described previously, as well as the unions with courtesans in the *Vaiśika* [section].
(p.364) 7. The *Aupaniṣadika* [section].

7.1. Formulas for making oneself fortunate, for subjugation, and aphrodisiacs. 7.1.1. The *Kāmasūtra* has been explained. 7.1.2. However, one who does not attain his desired goal through the methods stated therein [should resort to] the secret (*aupaniṣadika*)... [text fragment]
One should practice the secret methods [of the *upaniṣad*].
7.1.3. Beauty, virtue, youth, and generosity constitute the means of becoming beloved.
7.1.4. Anointing with an ointment of *tagara*, *kuṣṭha*, *tālīsa*, and *patraka* is a means of becoming beloved.
7.1.5. Having smeared a wick with these very same ingredients well-ground together, one should prepare collyrium in a human skull using sesame oil.
7.1.6. Oil prepared with *punarnavā*, *sahadevī*, *sārivā*, *kuraṇṭa*, and lotus leaves is used for anointing. 7.1.7. Garlands should likewise be prepared from those same ingredients.

7.1.8. By licking the powder of dried lotus (*padma*), blue water-lily (*utpala*), and *nāgakesara*, mixed with honey and ghee, one becomes beautiful. 7.1.9. Those same [substances], combined with *tagara*, *tālīsa*, and *tamālapatra*, used as an ointment (*anulepana*), [produce the same effect].
7.1.10. Or, having smeared the eye-fluid (*akṣitarakṣas*) of a peacock with gold...
Having anointed [the body], one should hold it with the right hand; this is the "Making Fortunate" (*subhagaṃ-karaṇa*) rite.
Likewise, [one should use] a jujube-seed gem (*bādara-maṇi*) and a conch-shell gem (*śaṅkha-maṇi*) among those [gems]. 7.1.11. [Ch inserts: ...among those...
In the same manner, he should cause them to practice the *Atharvaṇa* spells (*yoga*).
From the *Vidyā-tantra*, through the application of the *Vidyā*, the master should keep a female attendant who has reached puberty for a period of one year from another source.
Then, having kept her... [text fragment ends]
Thinking her to be averse [due to her youth], he became lustful for those objects of desire that were accessible to her; yet, he who was [intent on] her...
[was restrained].
The sage [or: in the case of a rivalry] should give much to him and dismiss him; this increases one's good fortune.

(7.1.13) A courtesan, once her daughter has reached puberty, should invite suitors according to their knowledge, character, and beauty, having determined that he who gives such and such wealth to her shall take her hand in marriage. (7.1.14) Saṃsādhya.
Having conversed with her, he should protect her.
(7.1.14) And she, while remaining unknown to her mother, should become exceedingly fond of the sons of wealthy citizens.
(7.1.15) Opportunities for meeting them occur during their acquisition of the arts in music halls, in the convents of female mendicants, and in various other places.
7.1.16. The mother shall cause the hand of the daughter to be taken by those who give as prescribed.
7.1.17. But if she does not obtain that much wealth, she herself shall declare to her daughter: "This was given by him even with only a portion of his own."
Or he may cause her, though already married, to regain the status of a maiden.
Or, having secretly united her with them while remaining himself unaware, he should then report the matter to the judges of law once it has become known.

7.1.20. A courtesan releases her daughter when she has been freed from maidenhood by a female friend or a slave girl, has mastered the Kāmasūtra, is established in the practical applications [of the art], and has reached a mature age and prosperity. Thus it is said. Having obtained...
The customs of the Easterners: 7.1.21. The taking of the hand [in marriage] entails a year-long period of non-transgression; after that, she may act according to her desire.

7.1.22. Even after a year has passed, if she is invited by one who has married another, she should set aside even her gain and come to him for that night—this is the rule for a courtesan. *pāṇi- [ch.]
The procedure for taking her hand and the rite for increasing good fortune.
(7.1.23) By this, the daughters of those who live by the stage are explained.
(7.1.24) But they should give her to one among them who is distinguished by musical instruments.
One should provide a distinguished musical instrument for the sake of [the deity]. Thus ends the "Making Fortunate" (Subhagaṃkaraṇa), the fifty-ninth chapter. (p. 366)
7.1.25. By applying a mixture of powdered dhattūraka, marica, and pippalī combined with honey to the penis, one achieves subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).

7.1.26. A flower whose petals have been blown away by the wind, a discarded garland from a funeral rite, and powder made from peacock bone—when these are applied as a dusting, they effect subjugation.

The powder of a *maṇḍalakārikā* (a woman who draws mandalas) who has died of her own accord, mixed with honey and *āmalaka* fruits, used for bathing, is a means of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). 7.1.28.
